prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads moisture levels from a DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 (analog resistive) using an MCP3008 ADC connected on the SPI0 hardware bus, with CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM), MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), and SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM); the sensor’s analog output is wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (CH0), and the program must sample once per second, logging the raw 10‑bit ADC value (0‑1023) to the console together with a timestamp, while providing robust error handling for any SPI initialization or transfer failures, ensuring that the SPI handle is closed and the driver library is terminated cleanly on all exit paths, and supporting graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the current from an MLX91219 Hall‑Effect Current Sensor (analog output) using an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1, with the sensor’s ADDR pin tied to GND, the sensor’s analog output connected to ADS1115 channel AIN0, SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM); configure the ADS1115 for single‑shot mode, single‑ended input on AIN0 (MUX = 100), a programmable gain of ±4.096 V and a data rate of 128 SPS, then every 500 ms read the 16‑bit conversion result using the appropriate API call with correct byte order, convert it to amperes, and log the current value to the console, while gracefully handling any I2C write or read errors and the case where the sensor is absent, and ensure that on receipt of SIGINT the program closes the I2C handle and invokes the library’s cleanup API call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces the AZDelivery KY-026 Flame Sensor Module and an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 running at 1 MHz, reading the digital output D0 of the flame sensor on GPIO4 (BCM) and routing the analog output A0 to MCP3008 channel 0 (single‑ended) while using the MCP3008 chip‑enable CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM); the program must initialize the driver, verify successful SPI open and transfer operations, and on each one‑second interval log a timestamped CSV row containing the current time, a boolean flame‑detected flag derived from the digital line, and an approximated temperature calculated from the analog reading to a file named flame_data.csv, while handling errors by skipping the entry and printing a diagnostic message if the sensor is absent or any SPI or file operation fails, and must ensure all resources are cleanly released on normal exit or when a SIGINT is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors a Keyes KY-026 Flame Sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM) as a digital input and an LM393‑based Heat Sensor whose analog output is read through an ADS1115 on I2C bus 1 using channel AIN0 (single‑ended), polling both every 100 ms with a 50 ms debounce applied to the flame sensor, and activates an active‑HIGH buzzer on GPIO27 (BCM) for exactly 2 seconds when both sensors indicate a fire condition at the same time; the program must log a fire event with a timestamp to a file named fire_log.txt when both conditions trigger, log “Flame detected!” if only the flame sensor is active, and log the temperature reading if only the temperature exceeds 60 °C, while performing thorough error handling that checks driver library initialization, I2C opening, ADC configuration writes, ADC reads, and log file creation, printing descriptive error messages to stderr for any failure, releasing any resources acquired so far and exiting with code 1 on any initialization error, and, if an ADC read fails due to I2C error or missing sensor, logging the error and continuing without crashing; the application should handle SIGINT by clearing a running flag so the main loop exits cleanly, and on exit it must turn off the buzzer, deregister any interrupt service routine, close the I2C handle, close the log file, and invoke the driver library’s cleanup call, using only the provided driver library (no other libraries), driving the buzzer with a simple digital write (no PWM), and compiling without warnings under gcc ‑Wall with no undeclared identifiers or implicit declarations.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples audio from two Analog Devices ADMP401 MEMS microphones using an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0, with chip‑select lines CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) and CE1 on GPIO9 (BCM), MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM), and SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM), while driving an LED on GPIO27 (BCM); the program must acquire one sample from each microphone every 1 ms for a total window of 100 ms (100 samples per channel), compute the RMS level for each channel, log the window timestamp together with mic1 RMS and mic2 RMS to a file named audio_events.csv, trigger the LED to stay on for 500 ms whenever either RMS exceeds a high‑level threshold, include error handling for SPI initialization failures and file I/O errors, and cleanly handle a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by turning the LED off and releasing all resources before exiting.

 * MLX90834 pressure sensor + ADS1115 ADC bridge reader for Raspberry Pi 4.
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   MLX90834 SDA -> GPIO2 (I2C1 SDA)
 *   MLX90834 SCL -> GPIO3 (I2C1 SCL)
 *   MLX90834 VDD -> 3.3 V
 *   MLX90834 GND -> GND
 *   ADS1115 VDD -> 3.3 V, VREF -> 3.3 V, AGND -> GND
 *   ADS1115 AIN0 -> MLX90834 AIN0
 *   ADS1115 AIN1 -> MLX90834 AIN1
 *   ADS1115 ADDR -> GND (I2C address 0x48)
 *   ADS1115 CLK -> GPIO11 (I2C clock)
 *   ADS1115 DOUT -> GPIO9  (I2C data)
 *   ADS1115 DIN  -> GPIO10 (I2C clock)
 *   ADS1115 CS   -> GPIO8  (I2C chip select)
 *   LED + 330Ω -> GPIO17 (active-high)
 *
 * Build: gcc -O2 -Wall -o mlx90834 mlx90834.c -lm
 */

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads motor current from a Melexis MLX91209 Hall‑effect current sensor (analog output) using an MCP3008 10‑bit SPI ADC on bus SPI0 CE0 at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0, with CE on GPIO8 (BCM), SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), sampling the sensor’s analog output on MCP3008 channel 0 (single‑ended) every 100 ms, logging each reading with a timestamp to a file named current_log.txt in append mode and flushing after every write, handling driver library initialization failures, SPI open or transfer errors, invalid ADC values and file I/O errors, asserting GPIO27 (BCM) HIGH to shut down the motor when the measured current exceeds 10 A, logging an OVERCURRENT event and terminating the program in that case, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly closing the SPI handle, closing the log file, resetting GPIO27 to LOW and invoking the library’s call() cleanup function.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the analog output of a Honeywell MICROceL MCO‑S4 CO sensor through an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 (1 MHz, mode 0) using CE0 on GPIO 8 (BCM), SCLK on GPIO 11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO 10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO 9 (BCM), sampling channel 0 once per second, and after each successful read logs the timestamp and voltage to a file named co_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,Voltage: X.XX V”; the program must check the return values of the required library API calls and the SPI transfer function, and if an SPI transfer fails it must log the error, wait one second before retrying, and ensure the alarm connected to GPIO 4 (BCM) is turned off for safety, while under normal operation it drives GPIO 4 HIGH when the measured voltage exceeds 2.5 V and LOW otherwise, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM it must close the SPI handle, close the log file, turn off the alarm, and invoke the appropriate library cleanup call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors methane concentration using a Honeywell MICROpeL Model 41000-020 Combustible Gas Sensor (analog output) interfaced through an MCP3008 ADC on SPI bus 0, channel 0, configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, with VDD/VREF tied to the Pi 3.3 V pin 1, DGND/AGND to any Pi ground, CLK on GPIO11 (SCLK, BCM), DOUT on GPIO9 (MISO, BCM), DIN on GPIO10 (MOSI, BCM) and CS/SHDN on GPIO8 (CE0, BCM); the program must read the sensor once per second, log each reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to “methane_log.txt” in append mode, and write a visible leak alarm to stderr whenever the concentration exceeds 1000 ppm, while checking the library’s API call() three separate times, as well as checking fopen() and localtime_r() for errors, logging any SPI transfer failure to stderr and continuing operation rather than crashing; it must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by closing the SPI interface, terminating the driver, and closing any open file handle, and must obey the constraint of not using the driver library directly, instead using the driver’s negative‑handle error codes without invoking the library’s API call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads pressure data from a Melexis MLX90830 analog pressure sensor using an ADS1115 16‑bit ADC on I2C bus 1, with SDA connected to GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL to GPIO3 (BCM) and the sensor’s analog output wired to ADS1115 channel AIN0, sampling at a rate of 1 Hz, validating that each reading falls within the 0‑100 kPa range, logging each valid pressure value together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named pressure_log.txt, performing thorough error handling for all I2C and ADC initialization and read operations, detecting and handling conditions such as a missing sensor or bus errors, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when the program receives a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C).

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces the analog Honeywell HIH-4602-A humidity sensor (which includes an integral thermistor) through an MCP3208 12‑bit ADC connected on the SPI0 bus using CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) as the chip‑select line, reads the humidity and temperature values, appends each reading as a comma‑separated line containing a timestamp, humidity, and temperature to a file named humidity_log.txt, and when the humidity value exceeds an 80 % threshold triggers an email alert via ssmtp; the implementation must include robust error handling for the ADC driver initialization, any SPI transfer failures, and all file I/O operations, and must also ensure that all resources are cleanly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads temperature data from a TMP36 analog temperature sensor using a MCP3208 12‑bit ADC on SPI0 with the device file /dev/spidev0.0 configured for mode 0, 8 bits per word at 1 MHz; the TMP36 signal output is connected to MCP3208 channel 0 (CH0, pin 1), chip‑enable CE0 is on GPIO8 (gpiochip4, BCM), SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO9 (BCM); the MCP3208 VDD and VREF are tied to 3.3 V; the program must perform a conversion at 1 Hz, validate the ADC reading, convert it to a Celsius temperature and log each sample as a line “timestamp,temperature_celsius” to temperature_log.csv, writing a header only when the file is newly created; it must check all SPI open, ioctl and transfer operations for errors, detect sensor‑absent or out‑of‑range conditions (valid range –40 °C to 125 °C), and implement signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully close the SPI device, release the GPIO lines and close the log file.

/*
 * PCF8591 AIN0 ADC monitor for Raspberry Pi.
 *
 * Reads the PCF8591 AIN0 channel (0-7) every 100 ms and prints each
 * sample to stdout.  The PCF8591 returns the result of the previous
 * conversion, so a dummy read is performed first to get the current
 * sample.
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o pcf8591_monitor pcf8591_monitor.c
 * Run:    ./pcf8591_monitor
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <sys/ioctl.h>
#include <linux/i2c-dev.h>

#define I2C_BUS        "/dev/i2c-1"
#define PCF8591_ADDR   0x20
#define PCF8591_REG_CONV 0x00
#define PCF8591_REG_CFG  0x01

static volatile sig_atomic_t g_running = 1;

static void sigint_handler(int sig)
{
    (void)sig;
    g_running = 0;
}

static int i2c_write_reg8(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t val)
{
    uint8_t buf[2] = { reg, val };
    if (write(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write to reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_reg8(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t *out)
{
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (reg select 0x%02X) failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, out, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read from reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the analog output of a YL‑83 rain sensor through an MCP3008 ADC connected on SPI0 using chip‑enable CE0 (bus 0, channel 0) in SPI mode 0 at 1 MHz, sampling once per second; the MCP3008 must be accessed in single‑ended mode on channel 0 with VDD = 3.3 V giving a full‑scale ADC value of 1023, and each sample should be mapped to a rainfall intensity level, then logged to stdout with a timestamp, the raw ADC value, and the computed intensity; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver, opening of the SPI device, and every subsequent API call, and if any SPI transfer fails it must print an error message and skip that reading, retrying on the next cycle rather than using stale data; finally, it must handle SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) to perform a graceful shutdown by closing the SPI handle and terminating the driver library.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the HL‑69 analog soil moisture sensor through an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 using CE0 (GPIO8, physical pin 24, BCM numbering) at a 1 MHz clock on channel 0, applies a hysteresis control that activates a relay‑driven pump on GPIO17 (active‑high, BCM) when the moisture reading falls below 30 % and deactivates it only when the reading rises above 35 %, publishes the moisture value every 60 seconds to the MQTT topic “soil_moisture”, and subscribes to the MQTT topic “pump_control” to accept “pump_on” and “pump_off” commands, while implementing robust error handling for SPI open or transfer failures, GPIO write failures, MQTT connection or subscription failures, and out‑of‑range sensor‑absent conditions, using the driver library v2 callback signatures, logging all events to syslog, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM the program cleanly turns the relay off, closes the SPI interface, disconnects from MQTT and terminates the driver library.
code:
/*
 * Soil Moisture Monitor with Hysteresis Relay Pump Control
 * Board:  Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
 * SPI:    SPI0, CE0 (GPIO8, BCM 24), 1 MHz
 * ADC:    MCP3008 on SPI0, channel 0
 * Relay:  PWM-controlled relay on GPIO17 (active-high)
 * MQTT:   Pub/sub to "soil_moisture"
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o soil_moisture soil_moisture.c -lrt -lpthread
 * Run:    sudo ./soil_moisture
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <sys/ioctl.h>
#include <linux/spi/spidev.h>
#include <pigpio.h>
#include <mosquitto.h>

#define SPI_DEVICE        "/dev/spidev0.0"
#define SPI_SPEED_HZ      1000000U
#define SPI_BITS_PER_WORD 8U
#define SPI_MODE          0

#define ADC_CHANNEL       0
#define PUMP_GPIO         17
#define PUMP_PWM_RANGE    255
#define PUMP_PWM_FREQ     1000
#define PUMP_ON_THRESHOLD 30.0f
#define PUMP_OFF_THRESHOLD 35.0f
#define PUMP_ON_TIMEOUT   60
#define PUMP_OFF_TIMEOUT  60
#define PUMP_TIMEOUT      -1
#define PUMP_ON_TIMEOUT_US (PUMP_ON_TIMEOUT * 1000000UL)
#define PUMP_OFF_TIMEOUT_US (PUMP_OFF_TIMEOUT * 1000000UL)
#define LOG_FILE          "soil_moisture.log"

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (Pi 3/4, 40‑pin header) that reads channel 0 from an MCP3008 10‑bit ADC over the SPI bus /dev/spidev0.0 using SPI mode 0, MSB‑first at 1 MHz, with CLK on GPIO11 (SPI0_SCLK, BCM), DOUT on GPIO9 (SPI0_MISO, BCM), DIN on GPIO10 (SPI0_MOSI, BCM) and CS on GPIO8 (SPI0_CE0, BCM); the program must perform proper error checking on every ioctl call, report any errors to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status if any initialization step fails, then repeatedly every 500 ms read the raw 10‑bit value from channel 0, compute the corresponding voltage assuming VDD = 3.3 V and VREF = 3.3 V, and print both the raw value and the calculated voltage, and finally handle SIGINT by cleanly closing the SPI device file descriptor before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the analog voltage on channels 0, 1, and 2 of an MCP3008 connected to SPI0 using chip‑enable 0, converts the 10‑bit values (with VREF = 3.3 V) to voltages, and appends a timestamped line with the three voltage readings to a CSV file named sensor_data.csv every 5 seconds; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, that the SPI interface opens successfully, that each SPI transfer succeeds, and that all file operations succeed, handling any error by reporting it and aborting cleanly, and it must install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that on termination it releases all resources by closing the SPI device and shutting down the driver library before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously samples the output of a MAX9814 electret microphone amplifier connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC via the SPI0 CE0 bus (/dev/spidev0.0) every 10 ms, uses the sampled ambient noise level to modulate two 3 V vibration motors with hardware PWM at 100 Hz on GPIO17 and GPIO27 (BCM numbering, each driven through a transistor), turns each motor off when the noise level does not exceed a threshold of 500, logs timestamps of any significant vibration events to a file named vibration_log.txt, implements robust error handling that logs any SPI initialization failures, ADC read errors (skipping the current iteration when a read fails), and file I/O problems, and ensures a graceful shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by stopping both motors, closing the SPI device, and terminating the driver cleanly.

/*
 * Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ – MAX9814 electret microphone amplifier
 * SPI0 CE0, MCP3008 ADC channel 0, two vibration motors (BCM)
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   MAX9814 VDD  -> 3.3 V (pin 1)
 *   MAX9814 GND  -> GND  (pin 6)
 *   MAX9814 OUT  -> MCP3008 CH0 (pin 3)
 *   MCP3008 CLK  -> GPIO11 (SCLK)
 *   MCP3008 DOUT -> GPIO9  (MISO)
 *   MCP3008 DIN  -> GPIO10 (MOSI)
 *   MCP3008 CS   -> GPIO8  (CE0)
 *   MCP3008 VDD  -> 3.3 V
 *   MCP3008 GND  -> GND
 *   MCP3008 CLK  -> GPIO11 (SCLK)

{

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that sequentially activates and deactivates four Songle SRD-05VDC-SL relay modules connected as a light sequencer on the GPIO digital output bus, using BCM pins 17, 22, 23, and 24 for relays 1‑4 respectively; the program must initially set all relay pins to inactive (LOW, assuming active‑high relays), then in an infinite loop activate each relay for one second, deactivate it, wait one second before moving to the next relay, and repeat this pattern indefinitely, while checking the result of every driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, etc.) for errors, providing clear comments throughout, and installing a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that, on exit, deactivates all relays and releases all GPIO lines; no SPI, ADC, temperature sensor, or logging functionality may be used and only standard C libraries together with the driver library may be employed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that drives an 8x8 common‑anode LED matrix over the GPIO bus, using the row anodes on GPIO 17, 18, 27, 22, 23, 24, 25, 4 (BCM) and the column cathodes on GPIO 5, 6, 12, 13, 19, 16, 26, 20 (BCM), scanning each row with an 800 µs delay, lighting an LED by setting the corresponding row HIGH and column LOW, and rendering two wave‑like animations that shift each frame, one moving left‑to‑right and the other right‑to‑left; the program must check every driver call, print descriptive error messages to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status on failure, and must handle a graceful shutdown on SIGINT by releasing all GPIO lines and performing cleanup, while adhering to the constraint of not using any driver library or deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that creates a wave‑like animation on an 8x8 common‑anode LED matrix driven directly over GPIO, with the row anodes connected to GPIO 2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, 9 (BCM) and the column cathodes to GPIO 14, 15, 18, 23, 24, 25, 8, 7 (BCM); the program must scan the columns left to right, clearing the matrix before each column by setting all column cathodes HIGH and all row anodes LOW, then for each column set the column cathode LOW and light the LEDs sequentially by setting the corresponding row anodes HIGH, observing a 150 ms delay between columns, checking the result of every GPIO operation and handling a chip‑open failure, using the driver library v2 API for all GPIO calls, and installing a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly releases all GPIO lines on exit, while respecting the hardware constraint that each column cathode is wired through a current‑limiting resistor (e.g., 220 Ω) and that a column lights when its cathode is LOW and all row anodes are HIGH, and the program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads proximity and ambient‑light data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 proximity/ambient‑light sensor attached to I2C bus 1, sampling every 500 ms, and appends each reading to a file named biometric_log.txt prefixed with an ISO‑8601 timestamp; the program must handle I2C read failures gracefully by logging the error and continuing, and if the sensor is absent or initialization fails it must print a diagnostic message to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status, while also installing a SIGINT handler that, upon receipt, cleanly closes the I2C handle, flushes and closes the log file, and calls the sensor’s library API call() before terminating.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads proximity and ambient light data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor attached to I2C bus 1, first verifying the sensor’s PART_ID before entering an infinite loop that samples the two measurements once per second, and logs each reading to a file named biometric_data.log in CSV format with an ISO‑8601 timestamp followed by the proximity value and the ambient light value, flushing the file after every write; the program must check the return code of every I2C read and write operation, handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors in a graceful manner, and install a SIGINT handler that, upon termination, closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and calls the sensor’s API call() function for proper cleanup.

/*
 * Si1145 Proximity & Ambient Light Logger for Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
 * Uses pigpio for I2C communication.
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   Si1145 SDA -> GPIO 2 (I2C1 SDA)

 *   Si1145 GND -> GND
 *
 * Build: gcc -o si1145_logger si1145_logger.c -lpigpio -lrt
 * Run:   sudo ./si1145_logger
 */

#include <stdio.h>

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that drives an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor over GPIO, using GPIO 17 (BCM) as the TRIGGER output and GPIO 27 (BCM) as the ECHO input, with a 1 kΩ/2 kΩ voltage divider on the echo line to protect the 3.3 V‑tolerant pins from the sensor’s 5 V logic; the program must issue a 10 µs trigger pulse, then wait up to 30 ms for the echo rise and up to another 30 ms for the echo pulse width, compute the distance, reject any reading outside the 2‑400 cm range, and every 60 seconds log the result to a file named distance_log.txt with an ISO‑8601 timestamp, including explicit error or timeout entries, and if the measured distance is below 15 cm also log the message “Time to water the plant!”; all driver calls must be checked for failure, handling the sensor‑absent case where the echo never rises and the timeout case where the echo stays high, and the application must catch SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all resources and closes the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the Adafruit APDS9960 sensor on I2C bus 1 to poll the device every 100 ms, detect proximity events and read the raw RGB color values, and whenever the proximity reading exceeds the threshold of 200 it appends a line containing the timestamp, the three RGB components and the proximity value to a CSV file named color_proximity_log.csv; the program must handle I2C communication errors by closing and reopening the bus and re‑initializing the sensor, and it must also catch SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, finalizes the CSV file, and releases any resources allocated by the driver.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that communicates with a Silicon Labs Si1182‑A‑GMR optical sensor over I2C (/dev/i2c‑1) to measure heart rate, reading the proximity data registers every 100 ms, converting each reading to beats‑per‑minute, and appending a line to a file named heartrate.csv in the form “timestamp,bpm” where the timestamp is an ISO‑8601 string; after each write the program must call fflush, and every i2c_smbus_* call must be checked for errors, aborting the program on any initialization failure but, if a read fails during the loop, printing a warning to stderr, skipping that sample and continuing; the application must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile running = false flag so the main loop can exit cleanly, after which it closes the I2C file descriptor, closes the CSV file and returns 0.

/*
 * Si1182-A-GMR heart-rate logger for Raspberry Pi 5
 * Uses pigpio for I2C communication.
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o si1182_logger si1182_logger.c -lpigpio -lrt
 * Run:    sudo ./si1182_logger
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define I2C_BUS        1
#define I2C_ADDR       0x50
#define CSV_FILE       "heartrate.csv"
#define SAMPLE_US      100000   /* 100 ms */
#define READ_DELAY_US  50000    /* 50 ms */

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the I2C bus 1 to communicate with an Adafruit VL53L0X Time‑of‑Flight sensor, first verifying the sensor’s presence at the documented value before any initialization, then configuring a falling‑edge trigger input on GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) with a pull‑up resistor; the program must wait for each falling edge, trigger a single distance measurement, poll the RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS with approximately a 100 ms timeout, and upon successful read log a timestamped distance in millimetres to a file named distance_log.txt in CSV format as “timestamp,distance_mm”, while providing robust error handling for every I2C transaction, handling sensor‑absent conditions and timeout paths, and must also install a SIGINT handler that on receipt performs a graceful shutdown by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and releasing all driver library resources on every exit path, all without using the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the TDK CH101 ultrasonic sensor on I2C bus 1 to measure distance, waiting approximately 50 ms after each trigger before reading the result and sampling every 200 ms; the program must initialize the driver and open the I2C bus, verify each write and read operation as well as the file open for logging, and on any I2C error print a diagnostic message and skip to the next sample without crashing, while logging each successful reading in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, <distance_mm>” to a file named distance_log.txt and also printing the same line to stdout, using a fixed‑size local buffer for the timestamp to avoid dynamic allocation, and it must handle SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) gracefully by exiting the sampling loop, closing the I2C handle, the log file, and shutting down the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses two TCRT5000 IR reflective sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO 17 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO 18 (BCM), to detect object proximity and log the binary readings (0 or 1) together with timestamps every 100 milliseconds to a file named obstacle_log.txt; the program must include robust error handling for any GPIO setup failures, and if a sensor read fails it should write an error message to stderr while continuing operation, and it must also handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that communicates with an Omron B5L‑LD50‑07050 3D TOF sensor over the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) to detect intrusion events within 1 meter and log the average distance; the program must send the documented 4‑byte command frame to request a measurement, wait at least 10 ms before reading the documented 15‑byte response, verify that byte 0 matches the documented header value, extract the 16‑bit big‑endian distance from bytes 11 and 12, sample the sensor ten times per cycle with a 100 ms delay between cycles, compute the average distance, and when the average is less than 1000 mm write a timestamp and the average distance to a file named intrusion_log.txt; all I2C open, ioctl, read and write calls must be checked for failure, and the code must gracefully handle sensor‑absent (I2C NACK) and bus‑error conditions, while also installing a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl‑C closes the I2C file descriptor and any open log files and releases all resources on every exit path.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that opens the I2C bus 1 device file (/dev/i2c-1) with full error checking, sets the Melexis MLX75030 Time‑of‑Flight sensor as the I2C slave using ioctl I2C_SLAVE and verifies that the device responds, then enters a loop that every 500 ms (using nanosleep) reads the distance measurement from the sensor and prints a line to stdout in the form “Distance: <value> mm”; if an I2C read fails the program must write a diagnostic message to stderr and simply continue to the next cycle without exiting, while if the sensor is not present at startup it must print an error and exit with status 1; a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must be installed so that pressing Ctrl‑C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and terminates the program with status 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads the Texas Instruments OPT3101 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, logging every 500 ms the distance measurement from channel 0, the ambient light value, and any error flags to the console, while implementing robust error handling for I2C communication failures such as a missing sensor or bus errors and guaranteeing that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using GPIO 17 (BCM) as the trigger output and GPIO 18 (BCM) as the echo input, issuing a 10 µs trigger pulse each cycle, waiting up to 200 ms for the echo rising edge and up to 200 ms for the echo falling edge, and performing one read per second; each valid measurement must be logged to the console together with a timestamp, while the code must handle driver library initialization failure, echo‑edge timeouts, and invalid pulse durations (≤ 0 µs or > 38 ms, the HC‑SR04 maximum range timeout), include a comment noting that the HC‑SR04 operates at 5 V and the Pi GPIO is only 3.3 V tolerant and therefore a 1 kΩ resistor must be used on the echo line within the library’s API call() that provides microsecond precision, and finally ensure graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by invoking the library’s API call() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads a range profile from a Texas Instruments IWR1443 mmWave radar over UART (/dev/serial0), decodes each data frame marked by an 8‑byte magic word header followed by 128 bytes of raw range profile data representing 64 little‑endian 16‑bit distance bins, checks whether any bin indicates a target within a 1.0‑meter distance threshold, and on detection logs an intrusion entry containing an ISO 8601 timestamp and the distance in meters to a comma‑separated file named intrusion_log.csv, while also activating an alert LED connected to GPIO 17 (BCM) for exactly 2 seconds; the program must handle UART initialization errors using the POSIX driver library, validate all I/O operations, gracefully manage sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and ensure clean release of all resources on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads obstacle detection data from an E18-D80NK IR sensor connected to GPIO 17, where the sensor presents an active‑low signal (0 when an obstacle is within the threshold distance and 1 otherwise), and drives a buzzer on GPIO 18 (active‑high) such that the buzzer is activated whenever an obstacle is detected and deactivated when the obstacle is removed; the program must poll the sensor every 100 ms via the GPIO bus, log each state transition with an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named obstacle_log.txt, rigorously check all driver return values and handle any errors such as chip open failure, line request failure, or read/write errors, and also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO lines and closes the chip.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TDK Chirp ICU-20201 ultrasonic time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1, reads the distance measurement every 100 ms, logs each distance together with an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named distance_log.txt, and monitors the reading so that when the measured distance falls below 10.0 cm the program asserts a GPIO alert on physical pin 17 (BCM 17); the implementation must handle all I2C read/write errors, detect the absence of the sensor, and manage any errors that occur while creating or writing the log file, and it must also cleanly release all resources—including I2C handles, the GPIO pin, and any driver state—when receiving a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a parking‑assistance system using the STMicroelectronics VL53L1X Time‑of‑Flight sensor connected on I2C bus 1; the program must poll the sensor every 100 ms in the main loop, check the return code of every driver, I2C, and file operation, and for each measurement append a line “timestamp,distance_mm” to a file named distance_log.csv, creating the file with a header row “timestamp,distance_mm” only when it does not already exist, while also printing a parking guidance message to stdout based on the measured distance—‘STOP’ for less than 300 mm, ‘APPROACH’ for 300‑600 mm, ‘SLOW’ for 600‑1200 mm, and ‘CLEAR’ for greater than 1200 mm; the application must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases the I2C handle, closes the log file, and de‑initialises the sensor driver on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the distance from a TDK InvenSense CH201 ultrasonic Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) every 100 ms, logs each timestamped distance and the corresponding LED blink frequency to stdout, and drives an LED connected to GPIO 18 (BCM) through a 330 Ω current‑limiting resistor to 3.3 V so that the LED blinks faster as the measured distance decreases, with each loop iteration performing exactly one half‑cycle of the LED blink (on or off) to keep the blinking smooth across samples; the program must check every driver and I2C call, retry any failed I2C read or write up to three times with 10 ms delays, and gracefully handle sensor‑absent conditions (I2C open failure) and bus‑error paths, and it must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that on termination cleanly close the I2C handle, turn off the LED, and shut down the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads distance data from a Melexis MLX75030 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at a 100 ms sampling interval, triggering each measurement with the required write command, waiting the appropriate delay, then reading the 2‑byte distance value in centimeters, and appending each reading to a comma‑separated file named distance_log.csv formatted as “timestamp,distance_cm”; the program must include robust error handling for I2C communication failures such as sensor absence, bus errors, or read/write timeouts, implement retry logic for transient errors, log any errors to stderr, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful termination when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces two TCRT5000 IR obstacle avoidance sensors on the GPIO bus, connecting sensor 1 to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO 27 (physical pin 13, BCM), polls each sensor every 10 ms, applies a 50 ms software debounce per sensor, and logs every state transition to a file named proximity_log.txt with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, the sensor ID (1 or 2), and the event type ('DETECTED' for a HIGH‑to‑LOW transition indicating an obstacle and 'CLEARED' for a LOW‑to‑HIGH transition indicating clearance); the program must check the return values of the library’s API call() three times as required, verify all file I/O operations, and on all exit paths—including graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM—ensure clean resource release by closing the log file and calling the library’s API call() to release the GPIO resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously measures distance from a TDK CH‑101 Time‑of‑Flight sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c‑1) by opening the I2C device with open(2), setting the slave address with ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), and using a helper that performs a combined write‑then‑read transaction to poll the MEAS_STATUS register with a 50 ms timeout before reading a successful distance measurement; after each successful read the program must wait 500 ms before the next sample, log an ISO‑8601 timestamp and the distance in millimetres to a CSV file named “distance_log.csv” with columns timestamp,distance_mm, checking the result of every open, ioctl, read, write and fopen call and, on any I2C failure, printing a diagnostic message including errno to stderr and skipping that sample without crashing; the application must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly close the I2C file descriptor, flush and close the CSV file, and then exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads zone distance data from a VL53L5CX ToF sensor connected on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1), configures the sensor for an 8×8 zone grid (64 zones), and logs all 64 zone distances to the console every 500 ms; the implementation must perform all I2C register reads and writes manually using standard Linux file I/O without any external driver library, include robust error handling for both I2C communication and sensor initialization, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling of SIGINT.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously polls a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 every 500 ms, initializes the sensor with a soft reset, configures its timing budget, and starts ranging, then uses the 16‑bit register access functions provided by the sensor’s driver to read distance measurements and opens the gate (GPIO 18 HIGH, GPIO 19 LOW) when an object is detected within 20 cm (200 mm) and closes it (GPIO 18 LOW, GPIO 19 HIGH) otherwise, logging each open or close event with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp to a file named gate_events.log, checking all driver and I2C return codes and handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully by logging the error, and implementing SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling to ensure that on any exit path the I2C handle is closed, the GPIO pins are reset, the log file is closed, and the appropriate library cleanup API is called.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses I2C bus 1 to communicate with a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor and controls a DC motor on GPIO17 (forward) and GPIO18 (backward) according to distance thresholds, triggering a distance reading on each rising edge of GPIO24 (BCM) via a pigpio ISR, where distances below 100 mm cause the motor to run forward, distances above 300 mm cause it to run backward, and values in between stop the motor, while logging every distance measurement and any motor state change to the console; the program must perform the VL53L1X register sequence of a soft reset write, a 1 ms delay, a start‑measurement write, then poll the status register until the data‑ready bit is set before reading the 16‑bit distance value, must check all driver and I2C return values, retry failed I2C transactions with exponential backoff, safely stop the motor if the sensor is absent or a bus error occurs, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly release resources by closing I2C handles, stopping the motor, and invoking the sensor’s API cleanup call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a proximity‑based interactive art installation using an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor connected on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1, GPIO 2/SDA and GPIO 3/SCL); the program must poll the touch status registers every 50 ms, monitor all twelve electrodes (ELE0‑ELE11), and when any electrode detects proximity it should drive a distinct 4‑bit LED pattern on GPIO 17 (BCM) as bit 0, GPIO 18 as bit 1, GPIO 27 as bit 2, and GPIO 22 as bit 3, while logging every proximity event to the console with a timestamp; it must validate every I2C read and write, verify the sensor is present by reading back a known register after a soft reset, and gracefully handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and finally ensure clean resource release on all exit paths by releasing all GPIO lines, closing the I2C and log file descriptors, and installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

 *
 * Wiring:
 *   SCD40 VDD  -> 3.3 V (Pin 1)
 *   SCD40 GND  -> GND  (Pin 9)

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature from an Analog Devices TMP05 digital temperature sensor by polling its PWM‑style output on GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7), measuring the high‑pulse width and total cycle width with a busy‑wait loop using microsecond‑resolution timestamps obtained from the library’s call() API, sampling once every 5 seconds and applying a 50 ms timeout on each edge wait; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly and that the log file “temperature_log.txt” opens in append mode, compute the temperature while guarding against division by zero if the low‑time (TL) is zero, flag any reading outside the valid range of –40 °C to +150 °C as an error, and after three consecutive failures write a “SENSOR MALFUNCTION” entry to the log, logging each valid reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp; it must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown by closing the file and releasing the driver library resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35‑DIS‑B sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented high‑repeatability, clock‑stretching‑disabled measurement command, validates the 8‑bit CRC for both the temperature and humidity words, and, after waiting at least 15 ms for the 6‑byte result, converts the raw values to degrees Celsius and percent relative humidity with the standard Sensirion formulas, then adds a sinusoidal offset of ±2 °C and ±5 % RH over a one‑hour period to simulate a greenhouse environment before logging each reading with an ISO‑8601 UTC timestamp to a file named “environmental_data.txt” every 5 seconds; if any I2C read/write or CRC check fails, the program must retry up to three times with a one‑second delay and, after exhausting retries, log NaN values, while also providing robust error handling for driver initialization, I2C open/read/write, and file open, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with the Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, sends the documented continuous measurement command, waits the approximately 45 ms conversion time, then reads the 9‑byte block containing pressure, temperature and scale factor each followed by an 8‑bit CRC‑8 checksum (using the polynomial and initial value documented for the sensor), validates those CRCs, converts the raw data to pressure in pascals and temperature in degrees Celsius with the sensor‑specified formulas, and logs a timestamp together with the pressure and temperature values to a CSV file named “airflow.csv” at a rate of one entry per second; the program must also detect and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C file descriptor and any open file handles.

{

        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

{
    log_file = fopen(LOG_FILE, "a");

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
static void dht11_start(void)
{
    if (gpioWrite(DHT11_PIN, 0) < 0)
        fprintf(stderr, "Error: gpioWrite(0) failed on start signal\n");
    gpioDelay(START_LOW_US);
    if (gpioWrite(DHT11_PIN, 1) < 0)
        fprintf(stderr, "Error: gpioWrite(1) failed on start signal\n");
    gpioDelay(START_HIGH_US);
}

static void dht11_stop(void)
{
    gpioWrite(DHT11_PIN, 0);
}

{
    if (bit < 0 || bit > 1)

    gpioDelay(BIT_DELAY_US);
}

{
    dht11_bit_wait(1);

    dht11_bit_wait(0);

{

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
/* DHT11 bit-bang helpers                                              */
/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
static void dht11_start(void)
{
    if (gpioWrite(DHT11_PIN, 0) < 0)
        fprintf(stderr, "Error: gpioWrite(0) failed on start signal\n");
    gpioDelay(START_LOW_US);
    if (gpioWrite(DHT11_PIN, 1) < 0)
        fprintf(stderr, "Error: gpioWrite(1) failed on start signal\n");
    gpioDelay(START_HIGH_US);
}

static void dht11_stop(void)
{
    gpioWrite(DHT11_PIN, 0);
}

static void dht11_bit_wait(int bit)
{
    if (bit < 0 || bit > 1)
        fprintf(stderr, "Error: invalid bit %d\n", bit);
    gpioDelay(BIT_DELAY_US);
}

static void dht11_bit_wait_high(void)
{
    dht11_bit_wait(1);
}

{
    dht11_bit_wait(0);

    dht11_bit_wait_high();

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the temperature from an STMicroelectronics LM75B sensor on the I2C bus once every second, stores the last 60 samples in a circular buffer in memory, computes the running average, and drives a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the fan is turned on when the average exceeds 28.0 °C and turned off when it falls below 26.0 °C; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, opening of the I2C interface, each I2C read, and each GPIO write, logging any failures to stderr and simply retrying on the next cycle without crashing, and it must handle SIGINT or SIGTERM by stopping the fan, closing the I2C handle, and terminating the driver library cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over I2C, waiting 45 ms after issuing the first measurement command before reading, then sampling once every second, reading exactly nine bytes each cycle and validating each CRC using the Sensirion CRC‑8 polynomial and its documented initial value; the program must log each reading to a file named airflow.log in CSV format with columns timestamp, differential pressure (Pa) and temperature (°C), print a warning to stderr whenever the pressure exceeds 5.0 Pa, robustly handle I2C read/write failures, CRC mismatches and the case where the sensor is absent, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C handle, close the log file and invoke the library’s call() cleanup function.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the temperature from an STTS2004 temperature sensor on the I2C bus, logs the temperature to stdout once per second, and drives an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the LED is set high when the temperature exceeds 28 °C and low when it falls below 27 °C; the program must check the result of every I2C read and every GPIO operation, and on repeated I2C failures it must log the errno details and exit cleanly, while handling SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing all driver library resources, closing the I2C file descriptor, turning the LED off, and then exiting.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that drives a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C, buffers CO₂, temperature and humidity readings in a thread‑safe circular buffer of capacity 100, and periodically persists the data to a timestamped CSV file in /var/log/scd40_data/ (creating the directory if it does not exist) with a header row, while logging any errors with timestamps to /var/log/scd40_error.log; the main loop must wait at least one second after issuing the start‑periodic‑measurement command before the first read, then read the sensor every five seconds, validating the CRC‑8 of each value using the polynomial and initial value documented for the device and, on any CRC failure or I2C read/write error, log the error and skip that reading; a separate logging thread must write the buffered records to the CSV file every sixty seconds, and the program must handle SIGINT by using a volatile sig_atomic_t running flag to stop the main loop, send the documented stop‑periodic‑measurement command, join the logging thread, flush any remaining buffered data to a final CSV file, close the I2C handle and cleanly terminate the driver without any resource leaks.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over the I2C bus, waiting at least 45 ms after each trigger for the measurement to complete and sampling once per second, reading the required nine bytes (two bytes of differential pressure followed by a CRC, two bytes of temperature followed by a CRC, and two bytes of scale factor followed by a CRC), validating each CRC‑8 using the documented polynomial and initial value, and logging each successful sample to a file named sdp810_log.txt in CSV format with columns timestamp, pressure_Pa, temperature_C; the program must handle I2C open, write, and read errors as well as CRC failures by logging the error and continuing operation, and it must install a SIGINT handler that on receipt closes the I2C handle, terminates any driver resources, closes the log file, and exits cleanly.

/*
 * SDP810 differential pressure sensor reader for Raspberry Pi 4 Model B.
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   SDP810 VCC  -> 3.3 V (pin 1)
 *   SDP810 GND  -> GND  (pin 9)
 *   SDP810 SDA  -> GPIO2 / I2C1 SDA (pin 3)
 *   SDP810 SCL  -> GPIO3 / I2C1 SCL (pin 5)
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o sdp810_reader sdp810_reader.c
 * Run:    ./sdp810_reader

#include <stdio.h>

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads pressure and temperature from a TDK ICP-10110 pressure sensor on the I2C bus, initializing the driver library and opening the I2C bus with proper error checking, then in a loop triggered every 5 seconds waits 10 ms after each trigger before reading the sensor, appends each sample to a file named environmental_data.txt in append mode flushing after each write, prefixes each line with an ISO 8601 timestamp and also prints the reading to stdout, handling any I2C read/write errors by printing a message to stderr and skipping that sample, and installs a SIGINT handler that sets a flag to exit the loop, after which the program closes the I2C handle, closes the file, and calls the library’s cleanup API call().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the TDK ICP-10125 barometric pressure sensor over I2C, retrieving exactly six bytes per read (two pressure bytes, two temperature bytes, and two CRC bytes) while checking every I2C syscall for errors, handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and verifying the CRC on each sensor read; after each trigger a 20 ms delay must be observed, the sensor should be polled once per second, and the result used to drive a warning LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) where the LED blinks at 1 Hz (500 ms on, 500 ms off) under normal conditions and switches to a 5 Hz pattern (100 ms on, 100 ms off) whenever the measured pressure falls below 95 000 Pa, with the GPIO line requested, set to output, and toggled accordingly; the program must also install a SIGINT handler that safely closes the I2C file descriptor and releases the GPIO line before exiting.
pinned_library: Linux i2c-dev for I2C, libgpiod for GPIO

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads ambient and object temperature from a Melexis MLX90614ESF-BAA infrared temperature sensor over the I2C bus, logs the timestamped readings to a file named temperature_log.txt every 2 seconds, and controls a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the fan turns on when the object temperature exceeds 30 °C and turns off when it falls below 28 °C; the program must validate driver library initialization, opening the I2C bus, and each I2C read/write operation, retrying any failed read up to three times with a 10 ms delay between attempts and skipping logging for invalid readings, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by closing the I2C handle, turning off the fan, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the Sensirion SHT40 sensor on I2C bus 1, issuing the measurement command, waiting at least 10 ms, then reading exactly six bytes, and streams the live temperature and humidity values to a local HTTP server on port 8080 using the library’s API call to serve an HTML page that displays the current temperature and humidity while clamping humidity to the range 0‑100 %; the implementation must include robust error handling for I2C communication such as sensor absence or bus errors with up to three retries per read, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path, handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals appropriately.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP102 on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, performs a measurement every 5 seconds, and appends each result to a timestamped CSV file named temperature_log.csv with lines formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,XX.XX”; the program must include standard headers such as errno.h and stdint.h to compile without warnings, check the success of all initialization and I/O calls, log any read failure to stderr while skipping that entry, and install a SIGINT handler so that when Ctrl+C is pressed the I2C handle is closed, the driver library is terminated, and the program exits cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC2010 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, polling the sensor’s MEASUREMENT_CONFIG register until bit 0 clears or a timeout of roughly 500 ms occurs, then outputs the readings to the console every five seconds; the implementation must check the result of every driver call, detect a missing sensor (NAK) and any bus‑error conditions, retry transient I2C failures only up to a defined maximum count, and include a clean shutdown triggered by Ctrl +C via a signal handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, closes the I2C handle, and invokes the library’s API call() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, waits approximately 45 ms for each measurement to complete, and logs to the console the raw 16‑bit pressure and temperature values every 500 ms; the program must open the I2C bus, verify that the driver library initializes correctly, check the result of every write and read operation, read exactly six bytes (two bytes pressure, one CRC, two bytes temperature, one CRC), validate each CRC‑8 checksum using the documented polynomial and initial value, handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions gracefully, and on receipt of a SIGINT perform a clean shutdown by closing the I2C handle and invoking the library’s cleanup API on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID‑controlled reflow oven using a MAX6675 thermocouple amplifier and a solid‑state relay, communicating with the MAX6675 over SPI0 (using either CE0 or CE1 as appropriate) and driving the solid‑state relay from GPIO17 (BCM numbering); the program must read the temperature from the thermocouple at a 1 Hz rate, update the SSR duty cycle based on the PID output (scaled 0.0 to 1.0) over a 1‑second period, log each temperature reading to a file named reflow_log.csv, load the target temperature profile from profile.txt where each line contains time_seconds,target_temp_celsius, apply robust error handling for all SPI communication and GPIO control including sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by handling termination signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID‑controlled greenhouse heater using a DS18B20 temperature sensor and a 12 V heater driven through a relay and hardware PWM; the DS18B20 data line must be connected to GPIO4 (physical pin 7) on the 1‑wire bus accessed via the w1‑gpio kernel module at /sys/bus/w1/devices/, the relay enable line to GPIO17 (physical pin 11), and the PWM duty control to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) using the hardware PWM channel, while the program must accept command‑line arguments specifying the desired temperature setpoint and the PID gains Kp, Ki, and Kd, read the sensor periodically, validate the CRC of each DS18B20 reading and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, compute the PID output, set the appropriate PWM duty cycle and relay state, and log every 5 seconds to a file named greenhouse.log a line containing the timestamp, average temperature, setpoint, PID output and PWM duty cycle; all I/O operations must be checked for errors, and the program must install SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that on any exit path cleanly release resources by turning off the relay, setting PWM to zero, closing any opened file descriptors or device handles, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, SDA on GPIO2 pin 3, SCL on GPIO3 pin 5) using the documented default address when SDO is tied to GND and falling back to the documented alternative address, applies the Bosch 64‑bit compensation formulas, rewrites the ctrl_meas register in forced mode each loop to trigger a new measurement, and appends a line to weather_data.txt every five seconds in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: XX.XX °C, Pressure: YYYY.YY hPa”, while checking every I/O call (open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, fputs) for errors, logging any sensor I/O failures to stderr and attempting to continue or exit gracefully, ensuring the sensor is powered from the 3.3 V rail only, and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to break the logging loop, close the I2C file descriptor and any open files, and exit with status 0.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the temperature from an LM75 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, performs the read once per second, stores each reading in an in‑memory circular buffer of capacity 60 samples protected by a mutex, updates a running average from the buffer, and drives an alert LED connected to GPIO18 (BCM) from a background thread so that the LED is turned on whenever the temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and turned off otherwise; the implementation must check the result of every I2C read/write and every GPIO initialization call, log any sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions to stderr, attempt to re‑initialize the hardware on such errors, and ensure that on all exit paths—including normal termination, error paths, and receipt of SIGINT—the program cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C file descriptor, releasing the GPIO line, and destroying the mutex.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces to a BMP180 sensor on the I2C bus using the documented address, reads the sensor’s calibration data and applies the Bosch compensation formulas to compute pressure in pascals, and toggles data logging on and off via a falling‑edge interrupt on GPIO27 with a 200 ms debounce; while logging is enabled the program must record a timestamp and the computed pressure to a file named pressure_log.txt every 2 seconds, must detect and recover from I2C communication errors and driver initialization failures, and must clean up all allocated resources and gracefully terminate when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier on SPI0 using CE0 (GPIO8 as chip‑select, GPIO9 MISO, GPIO10 MOSI, GPIO11 SCLK) at 2 MHz, drives a solid‑state relay connected to GPIO17 with a PWM signal to modulate a resistive heater so that a PI controller with anti‑windup maintains a target temperature (default 25.0 °C) while never exceeding a safe maximum duty cycle of 80 %, logs each measurement and the applied duty cycle together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named heater_log.csv, and implements error handling such that any SPI read failure or any MAX31855 fault condition (open circuit, short to ground or VCC) causes the duty cycle to be set immediately to 0 % and the error to be recorded in the log while the program continues running, and also catches SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that turns off the heater, closes the SPI interface, closes the log file, and terminates the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls the CPU temperature every 0.5 seconds and drives a common‑anode RGB LED attached to the GPIO bus with the Red cathode on GPIO17, Green cathode on GPIO18 and Blue cathode on GPIO27, using hardware PWM via the library’s API call() with a 0‑255 range and inverted duty (255 turns the channel off) while respecting the 3.3 V common‑anode supply and individual current‑limiting resistors; the program must open the temperature file, check the return value of the API call() each time it sets a PWM value and on any failure print an error message and exit with a non‑zero status, also handling fopen failure and short or failed reads by checking ferror, printing a diagnostic and skipping that update cycle, and on each loop iteration print to stdout the temperature in millidegrees Celsius together with the three PWM values; the LED color should be solid Blue (0,0,255) for temperatures below 40000 m°C, solid Green (0,255,0) for 40000‑59999 m°C, and solid Red (255,0,0) for 60000 m°C and above; a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, turn off all channels by writing a duty of 255, call the library’s API call() for cleanup, and allow the main loop to exit gracefully without calling exit() inside the handler, ensuring the file handle is closed on every code path and the program runs an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity and temperature from a DHT22 sensor connected on the 1‑wire bus with its data line on GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7), using the required start signal of pulling the line low for at least 1 ms, then captures the full 40‑bit response, validates the 8‑bit checksum, and posts the measured values as a JSON payload to http://yourserver.com/api/humidity via HTTP; the implementation must gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent, checksum mismatches, and network errors by retrying up to three times, and must ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses I2C bus 1 to communicate with a BMP180 sensor, configuring the sensor for oversampling setting OSS=3 and applying the full Bosch BMP180 integer‑only compensation algorithm, and that toggles data logging on and off with a push‑button connected to GPIO 4 configured for falling‑edge interrupts with the internal pull‑up; the interrupt handler must debounce using a driver‑library tick comparison of at least 200 000 µs, and when logging is enabled the program shall read pressure every 2 seconds, waiting the required 26 ms conversion delay, and append a timestamped pressure value in hPa to a file named pressure_log.txt, while printing a status message when logging is disabled; the code must check every I2C read/write return value, report any errors to stderr, fail cleanly if the sensor is absent or returns invalid calibration data, and on receipt of SIGINT must close the I2C handle and release all driver resources before exiting.

/*
 * DHT22 Humidity Reader for Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   DHT22 VCC  -> 3.3 V (Pin 1)
 *   DHT22 GND  -> GND  (Pin 6)
 *   DHT22 DO   -> GPIO4 (Pin 7, BCM 4)
 *   DHT22 CLK  -> GPIO5 (Pin 8, BCM 5)
 *   DHT22 DO   -> GND  (Pin 6)
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o dht22_humidity dht22_humidity.c -lgpiod
 * Run:    ./dht22_humidity [-s <url>]
 */

#define _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200809L

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <syslog.h>
#include <gpiod.h>

#define DHT22_BCM_PIN      4
#define DHT22_CLK_BCM_PIN  5
#define DHT22_DO_BCM_PIN   7
#define DHT22_VCC_BCM_PIN 3
#define DHT22_GND_BCM_PIN 6
#define DHT22_CLK_HIGH_US  40
#define DHT22_CLK_LOW_US   20
#define DHT22_READ_TIMEOUT_US 2000000   /* 2 seconds */
#define DHT22_RETRIES       3
#define DHT22_RETRY_DELAY_S  2
#define DHT22_MAX_RETRIES   3
#define DHT22_MAX_REPLY_LEN 256
#define DHT22_MAX_RESPONSE  40
#define DHT22_RESPONSE_LEN  (DHT22_MAX_REPLY_LEN + DHT22_MAX_RETRIES + 1)
#define DHT22_RESPONSE_BUF  (DHT22_MAX_RESPONSE + 1)
#define DHT22_RESPONSE_BUF_LEN (DHT22_RESPONSE_LEN + 1)
#define DHT22_RESPONSE_BUF_LEN_EXTRA (DHT22_MAX_REPLY_LEN + 1)
#define DHT22_RESPONSE_BUF_LEN_EXTRA_EXTRA (DHT22_RESPONSE_BUF_LEN_EXTRA + 1)
#define DHT22_RESPONSE_BUF_LEN_EXTRA_EXTRA_EXTRA (DHT22_RESPONSE_BUF_LEN_EXTRA_EXTRA + 1)

prompt: Write a C program for the Raspberry Pi 5 that actively manages the official Raspberry Pi 5 Active Cooler by reading the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and the current fan state from /sys/class/thermal/cooling_device0/cur_state, polling the temperature every 5 seconds, applying a tiered speed map where temperatures below 45 °C set the fan state to 0 (off), below 55 °C set state 1, below 65 °C set state 2, and 65 °C or higher set state 3 (maximum), first validating the cooling device’s max_state before any write, and writing the new state back to the same cooling_device sysfs entry only when the speed changes; each fan speed change must be logged with a timestamp to /var/log/fan_control.log, all file opens, reads, writes, and parses must be checked for errors with transient read failures simply causing the program to retry on the next cycle, and the program must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by setting the fan to state 0, logging the shutdown event, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a PID controller to maintain a target temperature of 50 °C by PWM‑controlling a resistive heater on GPIO18 using hardware PWM at 1 kHz with a duty range of 0‑100 %; the program must read the current temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier connected on SPI0 (CLK = GPIO11, CS = GPIO8/CE0, DO = GPIO9) at 500 kHz, acquiring 4 bytes per sample, and log every second to a file named heater_log.txt the measured temperature, the PWM duty cycle, and the PID output; the PID defaults are Kp = 1.0, Ki = 0.1, Kd = 0.01, and the controller must include error handling that parses the MAX31855 fault bits to detect open‑circuit, short‑to‑GND, or short‑to‑VCC conditions, logs any such errors, disables the heater and resets the PID state, and also enforces a failsafe that disables the heater if the reading exceeds 100 °C or falls below 0 °C; finally, the program must cleanly release resources on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the heater off, closing the SPI interface, and terminating any driver activity.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the GPIO bus to drive the PWM input of a Noctua NF‑A4x10 5V PWM fan connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12), polling the CPU temperature every 5 seconds and mapping the temperature linearly to a 25 kHz PWM duty cycle where temperatures of 40 °C and below correspond to 0 % duty, 70 °C and above correspond to 100 % duty, and values in between are interpolated accordingly; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, confirm that each PWM frequency and duty cycle call succeeds, and log each reading to a file named cooling_log.csv with a header and rows containing the timestamp, temperature in °C, and the PWM duty cycle percentage, while also handling any file I/O errors, and it must clean up gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the fan off and releasing all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with two Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensors on I2C bus 1, assuming the sensors are attached through a Sensirion SF06 multiplexer breakout or a comparable I2C hub, and polls each sensor once per second, reading three bytes from each (two data bytes followed by a CRC‑8 byte) while validating the checksum and retrying up to three times on any I2C error before giving up on that read; when a valid reading is obtained, the program must append a line to flow_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,flow1,flow2”, skipping the entry if the CRC check fails, and it must handle a clean shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by closing all I2C handles and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a magnetic rotary encoder built from two TMAG5110A1 Hall‑Effect latch sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with Channel A wired to GPIO17 and Channel B to GPIO18, configuring the pins as open‑drain outputs with internal pull‑up resistors enabled, implementing a 2‑bit quadrature state machine that resolves 360 pulses per revolution into a normalized angular position ranging from 0.00 to 360.00 degrees, logging each timestamped position change to a file named encoder_log.txt, providing robust error handling for both GPIO initialization and file I/O operations, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal by using the driver library’s cleanup facilities.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with the Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, samples the sensor every 100 ms, and logs each measurement to a CSV file named adpd144ri_log.txt with columns timestamp, red, and ir; the program must also monitor the infrared reading and activate an LED connected to GPIO17 (active‑high) whenever the IR value exceeds a threshold of 2000, while robustly handling I2C read/write errors and conditions where the sensor is absent, and it must cleanly release all resources—including the I2C file descriptor, GPIO lines, and the log file—on any exit path by catching SIGINT and SIGTERM signals for graceful shutdown.

/*
 * Seismic Event Monitor for Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+
 * Uses the Omron D7S-A0011 seismic sensor on I2C bus 1.
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   D7S-A0011 SDA -> GPIO2 (BCM)
 *   D7S-A0011 SCL -> GPIO3 (BCM)
 *   D7S-A0011 VDD -> 3.3 V
 *   D7S-A0011 GND -> GND
 *   Alert LED anode -> GPIO17 (BCM) via 330 Ω resistor
 *
 * Build: gcc -O2 -Wall -o seismic seismic.c -lthe_driver_library -lm -lrt
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <sys/ioctl.h>
#include <linux/i2c-dev.h>
#include <linux/i2c.h>

#define I2C_BUS        "/dev/i2c-1"
#define SENSOR_ADDR    0x10
#define ALERT_LED_PIN  17
#define VIBRATION_THRESHOLD 500
#define POLL_INTERVAL_MS 100
#define ALERT_DURATION_MS 1000
#define MAX_RETRIES     3

static volatile sig_atomic_t running = 1;
static int i2c_fd = -1;
static FILE *log_file = NULL;

static void signal_handler(int sig) {
    (void)sig;
    running = 0;
}

/*
 * Read a 16-bit value from the D7S-A0011.
 * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error.
 */
static int read_sensor_value(int fd, int16_t *value) {
    uint8_t buf[2];
    ssize_t n;

    /*
     * D7S-A0011:
     *   Bit 0-1  -> Vibration magnitude (0 = low, 1 = high)
     *   Bit 2-3  -> Seismic activity (0 = no, 1 = yes)
     *   Bit 4-5  -> Temperature (0 = low, 1 = high)
     *   Bit 6-7  -> Temperature (0 = low, 1 = high)
     *   Bit 8-9  -> Temperature (0 = low, 1 = high)
     *   Bit 10-11-> Temperature (0 = low, 1 = high)
     *   Bit 12-13-> Temperature (0 = low, 1 = high)
     *   Bit 14-15-> Temperature (0 = low, 1 = high)
     *   Bit 16-17-> Temperature (0 = low, 1 = high)
     *   Bit 18-19-> Temperature (0 = low, 1 = high)
     *   Bit 20-21-> Temperature (0 = low, 1 = high)

 *

 *   Si1175 SDA -> GPIO 2 (I2C1 SDA)

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that polls three Keywish 3‑Way Tracking Sensor (IR reflectance, digital GPIO) lines on the GPIO bus—left on GPIO2 (BCM), middle on GPIO3 (BCM) and right on GPIO4 (BCM)—every 100 ms, reads each digital value using separate driver calls, checks the result of every driver call (opening the device, getting each line, requesting each line, reading each line) and handles errors such as the device being absent or permission‑denied, then logs the sensor values to stdout in the exact format “L:<0|1> M:<0|1> R:<0|1>”, and ensures that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by installing a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) handler that terminates the program gracefully while still using only individual API calls rather than any bulk interface to maximize portability across driver versions.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that polls a TTP226 8‑channel capacitive touch sensor connected via GPIO, reading TP1 on GPIO5 (BCM), TP2 on GPIO6 (BCM), TP3 on GPIO13 (BCM), TP4 on GPIO19 (BCM), TP5 on GPIO26 (BCM), TP6 on GPIO12 (BCM), TP7 on GPIO16 (BCM) and TP8 on GPIO20 (BCM) every 200 ms, using a monotonic clock to timestamp each read and output a single line to the console in the form “[12.345s] CH1=0 CH2=1 CH3=0 CH4=0 CH5=0 CH6=0 CH7=0 CH8=0”, handling errors at every step by printing to stderr and exiting with a non‑zero status if the chip cannot be opened, a line request fails, or any individual line read fails, installing a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that gracefully shuts down by releasing all driver resources (lines and chip) before exiting, and including a comment with the compile command (e.g. “// gcc -o touch_poll touch_poll.c -lrt”).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the GPIO bus with hardware PWM at 1000 Hz and an 8‑bit range to smoothly fade a common‑anode RGB LED (Red on GPIO17 (BCM), Green on GPIO18 (BCM), Blue on GPIO27 (BCM)) between randomly chosen hues, selecting each new hue internally with rand() seeded from /dev/urandom, and performing a 50‑step linear interpolation over a 5‑second interval for each transition while clamping all channel values to the 0‑255 range; the program must verify the driver library initialization and check the return value of every library API call, logging any errors via syslog, and it must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that gracefully shut down by turning off the LED, releasing the driver resources, and closing syslog, with no networking or external message bus involved.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that opens the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 on BCM pins 2 and 3 to communicate with a TCS34725 color sensor, powers on the sensor (PON) and enables RGBC (AEN), configures an integration time of approximately 154 ms, and then enters a loop that polls the sensor every 200 ms, reading the calibrated red, green, blue and clear (C) values and printing those values to the console; the program must also control an LED connected to GPIO 17 (BCM) by setting the line HIGH when the calibrated red value exceeds a threshold of 200 and LOW otherwise, while rigorously checking every open, ioctl, read and write return value and attempting sensor re‑initialization on any read failure; finally, it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM and any other exit paths by cleanly releasing all resources, closing the I2C file descriptor, releasing the GPIO line, and powering down the sensor.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads acceleration data from a GY-45 MMA8451Q accelerometer on I2C bus 1, verifies the sensor’s identity by reading its identification register and confirming the documented value before proceeding, polls the sensor every 100 ms, and whenever the magnitude on any axis exceeds the 2.0 g threshold (with the default ±2 g range where 1 g equals 1024 counts) it turns on an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering) for 500 ms while logging each reading with a timestamp to a file named impact_log.txt; the program must handle I2C read/write errors gracefully and, on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM, cleanly release the I2C bus, GPIO lines and close the log file.
