Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads acceleration data from an Omron D7S‑0001 vibration sensor over the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1, samples the X, Y, and Z axes every 100 ms, and appends each sample to a file named vibration_log.csv with a header line “Timestamp,X,Y,Z” where the timestamp is an ISO‑8601 UTC string; the program must check the result of every open, ioctl, and read call, detect the documented sensor‑absent condition (for example when an I2C read returns the documented error value or fails), handle any bus errors gracefully without crashing, and on a read failure print a diagnostic message to stderr and simply skip that sample, while a SIGINT handler must be installed so that pressing Ctrl+C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file before the program exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors two TI DRV5032 digital Hall‑Effect sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with Hall sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and Hall sensor 2 to GPIO27 (BCM), configuring both inputs with internal pull‑ups enabled via bias flags, logging the millisecond‑precision timestamped state of each sensor to a file named conveyor_log.txt every 50 ms, and when both sensors read logic 1 the program must simulate halting the conveyor by printing a halt message; the implementation must include robust error handling for all GPIO access operations such as opening the chip, requesting lines, and reading values as well as for file I/O, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all driver resources cleanly on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64‑bit OS that continuously polls a GY‑45 MMA8452Q 3‑axis accelerometer on I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 at roughly 100 Hz (a 10 ms loop interval), first verifying the sensor identity by reading the WHO_AM_I register and exiting with an error message if the returned value does not match the documented value, then initializing the device by reading the control register, placing the sensor in standby, configuring the data rate to 100 Hz, and re‑enabling active mode; the program must read the six data registers in a single block read, combine the MSB and LSB of each axis, right‑shift by four to obtain signed 12‑bit raw X, Y, and Z values, compute the absolute tilt and, when a tilt exceeding 45 degrees is detected, append a line to a file named fall_log.txt (opened once in append mode at startup and flushed after each entry) containing a timestamp and the three raw values; all I2C system calls (open, ioctl, read, write) must be checked for failure with strerror(errno) printed and the appropriate action taken (exit or skip the iteration), and a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must be installed to close both the I2C file descriptor and the log file before terminating.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads calibrated magnetic field data from an Adafruit LIS3MDL Triple‑Axis Magnetometer over I2C at a rate of 10 Hz, applies the fixed offset and scale calibration constants and the ±4 gauss sensitivity of 0.146 mG per LSB before conversion, writes each X, Y, Z sample as a comma‑separated line to a single file named magnetic_log.txt that is opened once at start and flushed after every write, checks every I2C read and write for errors and retries the sensor initialization up to three times if needed, prints a metal‑detector alert to stderr whenever the total field magnitude exceeds 800 mG, and installs handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly close both the I2C file descriptor and the log file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously polls an E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensor connected on the GPIO bus, reading the sensor output from GPIO17 on gpiochip4 (BCM numbering) once every second, and when the sensor reports a LOW level indicating an obstacle within the configured ~30 cm detection range, logs to the console with timestamps the messages “Self‑parking sequence started” and, after the simulated routine completes, “Self‑parking sequence completed”; the implementation must use modern driver library APIs for opening the chip, requesting the line, reading its value and releasing resources, must check the return status of every library call and, if any call or the line is unavailable, exit gracefully with an appropriate error message, and must also install a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl‑C triggers a clean shutdown that releases the GPIO line and closes the chip on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously polls two Keyes KY‑032 IR obstacle‑avoidance sensors connected on the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (physical pin 11) and sensor 2 to GPIO27 (physical pin 13), using a single bulk‑read API call that reads both lines together at a 100 ms interval, interprets the active‑low output (0 = obstacle detected, 1 = path clear), logs the detection status together with a timestamp to the console on each poll, checks the return value of every driver call and handles the case where the API call or the GPIO lines are unavailable, runs in an infinite loop until interrupted, and on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT (Ctrl+C)—performs clean release of all resources, while compiling cleanly with ‑Wall ‑Wextra against driver version 2.0 or newer.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads gyroscope data from an Analog Devices ADIS16266 over the SPI bus using SPI0 CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) at a 1 MHz clock, operating in SPI Mode 3 with MSB‑first transmission on the /dev/spidev0.0 device, employing a two‑transfer read protocol where the address byte is sent with the MSB set followed by a 2‑byte read, then applying the scale factor of 0.02 deg/sec per LSB to obtain X, Y, and Z angular rates, logging those rates to the console every 100 ms, checking all SPI and GPIO initialization calls and handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including when a SIGINT is received.
pinned_library: libgpiod for the SPI CS line, with the Linux spidev interface for SPI communication

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the I2C bus 1 to communicate with an STMicroelectronics LSM6DSR IMU, reading the accelerometer and gyroscope X, Y, and Z axes every 100 ms and printing a single line containing the six values to stdout for each sample; the program must check the return value of every I2C operation, handle driver library initialization failure, I2C device open failure, WHO_AM_I register mismatch, any register write failures, and short or failed burst reads by printing an error message to stderr and exiting with a non‑zero status, avoid using hard‑coded sleeps that ignore errors, and install a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl +C triggers a clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and calls the appropriate library cleanup function before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that opens I2C bus 1 on the SDA pin (GPIO2, BCM) and SCL pin (GPIO3, BCM) to communicate with an Adafruit FXOS8700 breakout board, first confirming the device is present by reading its identification register and comparing the result to the documented value, then initializing the sensor and entering a loop that every 100 ms reads a 12‑byte combined block containing six bytes of 14‑bit left‑aligned accelerometer data followed by six bytes of 16‑bit magnetometer data, extracts the raw X, Y, Z values for both the accelerometer and magnetometer and prints them to the console, while checking each I2C call for errors, retrying on transient read failures, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM all resources—including the I2C handle and any driver state—are cleanly released.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads acceleration data from an ADXL345 accelerometer over I2C, evaluates the tilt angle and, whenever the tilt exceeds a threshold of 30.0 degrees, writes a timestamped entry to /var/log/tilt_events.log, performing this sampling and logging cycle every 100 ms; the implementation must include robust error handling that explicitly detects and manages I2C communication failures, sensor‑absent conditions, and bus‑error paths, and must guarantee clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper handling of a Ctrl+C interrupt signal.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a smart home lighting system with a sunrise/sunset fade driven by a 24‑hour schedule file named lighting_schedule.txt, where each line follows the format HH:MM:SS,relay_number,on/off; the program must control four relay‑controlled lamp actuators connected to GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22 (BCM numbering), checking the schedule file every second, and when a transition is required it must perform a 1800‑second (30‑minute) fade using 100 Hz PWM to vary lamp brightness with a duty cycle ranging from 0 to 100; it must handle file read errors, GPIO initialization failures, and invalid schedule entries gracefully, and must install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly turn off all relays and release GPIO resources on exit while avoiding any non‑reentrant functions such as fopen or localtime inside those handlers.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a rudimentary theremin by reading distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor and mapping it to a PWM buzzer frequency, using GPIO23 (BCM) for the trigger output, GPIO24 (BCM) for the echo input, and GPIO18 (BCM) for the PWM buzzer output; the program must issue a 10 µs trigger pulse via the library’s API, obtain microsecond‑precision echo timing through the same API, run a main loop at roughly 50 Hz while enforcing a minimum 60 ms gap between successive measurements, clamp the computed frequency to the buzzer’s valid range before applying it, provide robust error handling for driver initialization and HC‑SR04 readings—including detection of a missing sensor and timeout conditions—with any failures logged to stderr, and clean up gracefully on SIGINT by silencing the buzzer and deinitializing the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that drives a common‑anode RGB LED using hardware PWM at a 1 kHz frequency on the BCM pins where red is on GPIO17, green on GPIO22 and blue on GPIO27, generating a smooth color transition that reflects a simulated proximity value ranging from 0.0 to 1.0 (for example a sine‑wave function over time) rather than any external input, while handling driver library initialization errors gracefully, checking the result of every GPIO operation, and ensuring that on all exit paths—including a SIGINT interrupt—the LED is turned off and the PWM resources are released with the appropriate library call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads angular velocity from an MPU‑6050 gyroscope over the I2C bus /dev/i2c‑1 using the documented device address, with SDA connected to GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL to GPIO3 (BCM), samples the sensor every 100 ms, and appends to a file named gyro_log.txt a timestamp followed by the x, y, and z axis values in degrees per second; the program must robustly handle all I/O and I2C errors by checking the return values of open, ioctl, read and write calls and must also detect and manage the case where the sensor is absent, and it should cleanly close all file descriptors and terminate gracefully when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM, while no network logging or configuration file parsing is required.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a button wired to GPIO17 (BCM) with its internal pull‑up enabled and active‑low, debounces it with at least a 50 ms interval, and on each valid press triggers a musical doorbell by playing a stored melody from a const melody lookup table through a piezo buzzer connected to the hardware PWM0 output on GPIO18 (BCM) using the library's API call() to generate tones at a 50 % duty cycle for volume; the ISR must be non‑blocking and set a volatile flag that the main loop checks to start or, if a second press occurs during playback, gracefully stop the melody, and the program must include proper error handling for every the driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call), as well as handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown by stopping PWM, releasing resources, and calling the library's API call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads edge events from an SW‑420 vibration sensor module whose digital output (active‑high) is wired to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11), using the library’s API call for edge‑triggered polling on both rising and falling edges (the same library’s API call must be invoked three times as required), accepts an optional poll timeout in milliseconds as a single command‑line argument defaulting to 1000 ms, maintains a sliding window of the last five events and, whenever three or more of those events are HIGH, prints an “EARTHQUAKE ALERT” message together with the current ISO‑8601 timestamp, logs every edge event to a persistently open file named vibration_events.log with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and the raw value (0 or 1) flushing or fsyncing after each write, handles any file open or write errors gracefully by printing diagnostics to stderr without terminating, checks the return value of every driver library call and system call for errors, and installs a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop can exit cleanly, releasing the GPIO line and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads calibrated magnetic‑field data from an LSM303DLHC magnetometer connected on the I2C bus /dev/i2c‑1 using the documented 7‑bit address, with SDA wired to physical pin 3 (GPIO2/BCM) and SCL to physical pin 5 (GPIO3/BCM), samples the sensor once per second, applies the hard‑iron calibration offsets X_OFFSET = 10, Y_OFFSET = ‑5, Z_OFFSET = 20, computes a heading in degrees and maps it to one of the eight compass directions (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW), logs each sample to a file named mag_log.csv with a header row of “Timestamp, Calibrated X, Calibrated Y, Calibrated Z, Heading” if the file does not already exist and appends rows containing the timestamp, calibrated X, Y, Z values and numeric heading, prints the compass direction and numeric heading to the console, checks the result of every open, ioctl, read, write, and fopen call and, on any I2C read failure, writes a diagnostic message to stderr and skips that sample without crashing, and installs a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file and frees all resources on every exit path.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM) configured with a pull‑down resistor and, on each valid touch, toggles a 5 V relay attached to GPIO17 (BCM), ensuring that touches are accepted only if at least 200 ms have elapsed since the previous one by implementing software debounce inside the interrupt service routine, logs every state change to a file named relay_log.json as a JSON object containing an ISO 8601 timestamp and the relay_state field set to “ON” or “OFF”, checks the return value of every driver library call and aborts cleanly if any call fails, and installs a SIGINT handler that, upon termination, forces the relay OFF, appends a final OFF entry to the log, invokes the required library cleanup call, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a smart irrigation system which sequentially activates four 5 V relay modules connected to GPIO17, GPIO23, GPIO24 and GPIO25 (BCM numbering) based on a simulated soil moisture value generated by rand() seeded once at startup and ranging from 0 to 100; every 10 seconds the program must obtain a new moisture reading, and if the value is below 30 it must drive each relay low (active‑low, with an inactive high level of 1) for exactly 5 seconds with a 1‑second gap between relays, appending to an irrigation_log.txt file (opened in append mode and flushed after each write) a line containing an ISO‑8601 timestamp, the relay number and the moisture level; every driver library call and file operation must be checked and any failure reported to stderr, and the program must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that deactivate all relays, release the GPIO lines, close the log file and exit cleanly, while ensuring that each GPIO line is requested as an output only once.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements an automated plant watering system using two SG90 servo motors controlled via the library's API call, with the valve servo attached to GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM) and the nozzle servo attached to GPIO18 (physical pin 12, BCM); the program must read a simulated soil moisture value that cycles every 1 second through the hard‑coded sequence 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 and, when the moisture is below 50, open the valve by issuing a library's API call with a pulse width corresponding to 90 degrees (≈1500 µs) then sweep the nozzle through the five angles 0, 45, 90, 135 and 180 degrees (pulse widths 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500 µs) spending 2 seconds on each step, hold the spray for 5 seconds, close the valve to 0 degrees (500 µs) and then wait 5 seconds before the next cycle, while if the moisture is 50 or above the watering cycle is skipped; every library's API call must have its return value checked, be retried up to three times on failure with a 100 ms backoff and cause the program to exit on unrecoverable error, abort the watering cycle if the valve fails to open, print a critical warning if it fails to close, and log the error but continue to the next angle if a nozzle position fails; the program must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set volatile sig_atomic_t flags, and in the signal handler stop both servos by calling the library's API call with a zero argument, then invoke the library's API call cleanup function and exit cleanly, never invoking any GPIO functions before or after the library's API call in the handler; finally the code should be compiled with gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o watering watering.c -lthe driver library -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the X, Y, and Z angular velocities from an MPU‑6050 gyroscope connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1) using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM) at the documented address, samples the data at 10 Hz, and appends each reading to a file named gyro_log.txt in CSV format containing a timestamp followed by the X, Y, and Z values; the program must check the result of every I2C system call, provide explicit handling for cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error, and must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that ensure all open file descriptors and any other resources are cleanly released on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that drives a 28BYJ-48 unipolar stepper motor through an L293D driver to lock and unlock a simulated door on button press, using GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27 and GPIO22 (BCM) for the L293D IN1‑IN4 coil inputs, a LOCK button on GPIO24 (BCM) and an UNLOCK button on GPIO23 (BCM) with internal pull‑ups and active‑low logic, implementing full‑step (single‑coil) excitation and rotating the motor 512 steps clockwise for a LOCK press and 512 steps counter‑clockwise for an UNLOCK press with a 3 ms inter‑step delay, debouncing the button reads so a single press does not trigger multiple rotations, de‑energizing all coils after each rotation to reduce power consumption and heating, printing console messages for lock, unlock and any errors, checking the return value of the library’s API call() after every operation and reporting an error on failure, and handling SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) gracefully by de‑energizing the coils and calling the library’s API call() before exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (64‑bit, Bookworm) that reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor and logs the result every second to a file named distance_log.txt opened in append mode and kept open for the lifetime of the program; the trigger line must be requested as an output on GPIO17 (BCM) and the echo line as an input on GPIO18 (BCM) with active‑high polarity, the sensor’s 5 V echo output being reduced to 3.3 V by a voltage divider or level shifter before reaching the Pi, the program must generate a 10 µs trigger pulse, wait for the rising edge of the echo with a 50 ms timeout, then wait for the falling edge with the same timeout, compute the distance, and write the value to the log, pausing at least 60 ms between measurements and sampling at a 1 s interval; on any timeout or driver call failure the program must write “‑1” to the file and print an error message to stderr, and any GPIO initialisation failure must be reported to stderr, while SIGINT or SIGTERM must be caught to cleanly release all driver resources and close the log file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads distance from a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor attached to I2C bus 1 using the documented default address, polls the sensor every 100 ms, prints the current distance to stdout, and drives a relay connected to GPIO18 (BCM) so that the relay is set HIGH when the measured distance is less than or equal to 50 cm and LOW otherwise, while checking every driver and I2C return value, handling cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error by logging all such errors to stderr, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT the program cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C interface, setting the relay pin low, and terminating the driver usage.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the angular velocity from an MPU‑6050 gyroscope over the hardware I2C bus /dev/i2c‑1 using the documented device address, with SDA connected to GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL to GPIO3 (BCM); the program must continuously acquire the x, y, and z axis rotation rates and log those three values to the console, while checking the result of every I2C read and write system call and handling any sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, and it must also install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that all resources are cleanly released on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements an automated plant watering system by sequentially activating four 5 V relay modules connected to GPIO17, GPIO18, GPIO27 and GPIO22 (BCM numbers, physical pins 11, 12, 13, 15); the program must open the library’s API, request all four lines as outputs with active‑low semantics, set all lines HIGH (inactive) at startup, then in a main loop that polls every 60 seconds activate each relay in turn for exactly 5 seconds, repeating the whole sequence once every 86 400 seconds (24 hours) beginning immediately on launch, log the start time of each full cycle to a file named watering_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS”, check the result of every library call and every file I/O operation handling errors including the case where the GPIO chip cannot be opened, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that releases all GPIO lines, closes the chip and exits cleanly; the code must be compiled with gcc ‑o watering watering.c ‑lgpiod and must not use any deprecated driver interface.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that creates a smart lighting sunrise effect by gradually increasing the intensity of four SRD-05VDC relay modules over a 30‑minute period, stepping the change every second and using a 1 kHz hardware PWM signal with duty cycles from 0 to 255 applied simultaneously to the relays connected to GPIO17, GPIO18, GPIO27 and GPIO22 (BCM numbering, equivalent to wiringPi pins 0, 1, 2, 3); the program must log every event with timestamps to a file named smart_lighting.log, verify each GPIO pin mode setup and check the library’s API call() return values, handle any PWM initialization failures gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads angular velocity from an MPU‑6050 gyroscope on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, with SDA connected to GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL to GPIO3 (BCM), sampling at 20 Hz (a 50 ms period), storing each timestamped X, Y, and Z reading in a 100‑entry in‑memory circular buffer, continuously checking every driver call for errors, printing an error and exiting if I2C initialization fails, and if a read fails attempting re‑initialization up to three times before exiting; the program must drive an LED on GPIO17 (BCM) such that the LED is turned on whenever the absolute value of any axis exceeds 250 deg/s and turned off when all axes are below that threshold, without configuring the accelerometer, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown by closing the I2C handle, setting the LED GPIO low, and invoking the library’s cleanup call.

/*
 * ADXL345 free-fall detector for Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+
 * Uses pigpio for I2C and GPIO27.
 *
 * Wiring:

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a GPIO‑connected HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor (TRIG on GPIO4 BCM, ECHO on GPIO18 BCM) to measure distance in an interrupt‑driven fashion and log each valid reading to a file named distance_log.txt in CSV format “timestamp_ns,distance_cm”, running indefinitely; the program must generate a 10 µs trigger pulse on the TRIG line, wait 200 ms between trigger cycles, capture the echo pulse width with rising‑edge and falling‑edge interrupt callbacks protected by a mutex, discard any measurement whose pulse width exceeds 23 200 µs (approximately 4 m, the sensor’s maximum range), treat a missing echo within 100 ms after a trigger as a timeout error, handle driver library initialization failure, file open failure, invalid pulse widths and sensor timeouts, record timestamps with nanosecond precision using a 32‑bit tick counter that wraps roughly every 71.6 minutes, and install a SIGINT handler that on termination cancels the callbacks, closes the log file, terminates the driver library and destroys the mutex.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads the Adafruit LIS3DH accelerometer on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, detects a free‑fall when the measured acceleration magnitude falls below 0.2 g, then detects an impact when the magnitude rises above 1.5 g (allowing the free‑fall and impact thresholds to be overridden by optional command‑line arguments), and upon detecting the impact activates a buzzer connected to GPIO17 (BCM) for exactly one second; the implementation must initialize the I2C interface and the sensor driver with full error checking, retry any I2C communication failure up to three times, handle the absence of the sensor or bus errors gracefully, and ensure that on receipt of SIGINT the program performs a clean shutdown releasing all resources and leaving the GPIO and I2C bus in a safe state.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the GPIO bus to drive two 28BYJ‑48 stepper motors with ULN2003 driver boards, configuring Motor 1 (X‑axis) IN1 on GPIO4 (BCM), IN2 on GPIO17 (BCM), IN3 on GPIO27 (BCM) and IN4 on GPIO22 (BCM), and Motor 2 (Y‑axis) IN1 on GPIO5 (BCM), IN2 on GPIO6 (BCM), IN3 on GPIO13 (BCM) and IN4 on GPIO19 (BCM) as outputs, employing a 4‑step wave drive sequence (single‑coil excitation) with a 1000 µs step delay, calculating the required steps from the 28BYJ‑48’s 1/64 gear ratio and 2048 steps per revolution to trace a 50 mm square, checking that the driver initialization succeeds and verifying each API call, handling any motor movement failures gracefully, and installing a SIGINT handler that safely stops both motors, sets all GPIO pins low and releases resources before termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the Adafruit LIS3DH accelerometer on the I2C bus, reading acceleration at a 10 Hz interval (every 100 ms) and configuring the sensor for a ±2 g range, high‑resolution 12‑bit left‑justified mode with a 100 Hz output data rate, supporting only a single sensor; the program must accept optional command‑line arguments “‑a” for the I2C address in hex and “‑t” for a threshold in g (default 2.0 g, must be > 0), validate that the address falls within the documented range, and on any axis exceeding the threshold log a line containing a timestamp and the three axis values to /var/log/high_acceleration.log before invoking “sudo shutdown -h now”; it must handle I2C open or configuration errors by performing cleanup (closing the bus and terminating the driver library) and exiting with code 0 in non‑hardware environments, handle sensor read errors by returning zeros and continuing, use the library’s API calls for I2C operations and single‑byte register writes (which return 0 on success), and install a SIGINT handler that gracefully terminates by closing I2C and shutting down the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors two Sensirion SLF3S‑1300F liquid‑flow sensors (40 ml/min version) connected to I2C bus 1, using the documented I2C addresses for sensor 1 and sensor 2, and controls a safety relay on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering, active‑high) with a 100 ms polling loop; each iteration must read three bytes from each sensor, validate the CRC‑8 using the documented polynomial, initial value and no final XOR, and if a read returns fewer than three bytes or the CRC check fails, a warning is written to stderr and the cycle is skipped without changing the relay state, otherwise the flow rates are logged with millisecond timestamps to flow_log.txt in append mode with an immediate flush, and if both reads succeed and either sensor reports a flow below 5.0 ml/min the relay is energized (write 1) and otherwise de‑energized (write 0) when both are at or above 5.0 ml/min; the program must check the library’s API return codes for opening I2C bus 1 with flags 0 for each sensor, verify that the start‑measurement command write (the documented two‑byte sequence) returns 0 for each sensor, and also verify the GPIO 18 configuration call’s return code, performing full cleanup of any partially‑initialized resources on any failure, and on shutdown triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM it must de‑energize the relay, close any open I2C handles, call the library’s cleanup function, and print a shutdown message, while compiling cleanly with gcc ‑Wall ‑Wextra.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors the Seeed Studio Rain Sensor v1.0 digital output on GPIO 17 (BCM) configured as an input with a pull‑up, polling every 200 ms over the GPIO bus, and drives a DC motor window actuator through an L298N driver using ENA on GPIO 22 (BCM), IN1 on GPIO 23 (BCM) and IN2 on GPIO 24 (BCM); the sensor pulls its DO pin low when rain is present and high when dry, so the program must detect a rising‑edge (dry‑to‑wet transition) and, on that edge only, start the close‑window sequence by setting ENA high, IN1 high, IN2 low, holding the motor for exactly 5 seconds using the library’s API call() or usleep() (no busy‑wait), then stopping the motor by setting ENA low and both IN1 and IN2 low while verifying each call, logging all events with syslog (facility LOG_USER, identifier “rain_window”) as LOG_INFO for startup, rain detection, motor start/stop and shutdown and using LOG_ERR or LOG_WARNING for any call failures, suppressing further triggers until the sensor reads dry for at least three consecutive polls (≈600 ms), and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that stops the motor (all calls LOW), calls the library’s API call() to clean up, closes syslog and exits cleanly, with every library API call return checked and logged, all within a single‑process design without forks.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the GPIO bus to control a hobby servo acting as a door‑lock actuator based on two momentary push‑buttons, with the servo connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12, BCM 18), the lock button to GPIO 21 (BCM) and the unlock button to GPIO 22 (BCM), both buttons wired to ground when pressed and therefore requiring internal pull‑up resistors to be enabled; the program must poll the buttons in a tight loop with a small sleep to keep CPU usage low, implement debouncing by waiting for the button release plus a short delay so that a single press is not registered multiple times, drive the library’s API call() with a 2000 µs pulse width when the GPIO 21 button is pressed to lock, a 1000 µs pulse width when the GPIO 22 button is pressed to unlock, and output status messages to stdout for lock, unlock, and shutdown events, verify that the API call() returns success for both pulse‑width commands and exit with an error message on failure, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that stops the servo by sending a pulse width of 0, calls the API call() one final time, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a PIR motion sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7, BCM 4) using a 100 ms polling interval and, on each rising edge, activates a relay‑controlled 12 V LED floodlight connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM 17) for exactly 60 seconds before turning it off, while appending activation events with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and deactivation events with a timestamp and the measured duration in seconds to a file named security_log.txt; the program must verify that the driver library is successfully initialized, check the return code of every library API call as well as the result of every fopen, fprintf and fclose operation, and if any file operation fails it must turn off the floodlight before exiting, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly turns off the floodlight, releases the driver library resources, and exits with code 0, ensuring that the floodlight is OFF on all exit paths and that no driver library is used directly in the code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 (using the documented address) to toggle a relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM) only on a fresh rising‑edge touch of electrode 0, applying a 200 ms debounce to that electrode, performing a full MPR121 initialization that includes a soft‑reset, configuration of baseline filtering (MHD, NHD, NCL, FDL) to the documented values, setting the debounce to the documented value, configuring FFI, SFI and CDT to the documented values, enabling auto‑config with the documented range, and enabling exactly 12 electrodes as documented; the program must set the relay to a known OFF state at startup and also ensure it is OFF on shutdown, must implement robust error handling for every driver library and I2C call by checking return values and handling sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path, including handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the GPIO bus to control a servo motor on BCM GPIO17 and read a PIR sensor on BCM GPIO4, listening for TCP connections on port 5000; the program must accept commands of the form “the library's API call <angle>” where <angle> is 0‑180 and generate a software PWM signal at 50 Hz with a 1‑2 ms pulse width to position the servo, and also respond to the command “PIR” by sending back “PIR:0” or “PIR:1” over the socket, while logging all events, commands, and errors to both syslog (LOG_USER facility) and a file named security.log with ISO 8601 timestamps, checking the result of every driver library call, socket syscall, and file I/O operation and, if GPIO initialization fails, logging the error and exiting with a non‑zero status; the code must include <stdarg.h> for variadic functions so it compiles cleanly with -Wall -Wextra, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all driver resources, closes the socket and the log file.

 * RPM monitor for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using an A3144 Hall-effect sensor
 * and a two-pole magnet on the motor shaft.
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   A3144 VCC  -> 3.3 V (pin 1)
 *   A3144 GND  -> GND  (pin 6)
 *   A3144 OUT  -> GPIO17 (BCM 17, physical pin 11)
 *   Magnet N/S  -> GPIO17 (BCM 17)
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o rpm_monitor rpm_monitor.c -lrt
 * Run:    ./rpm_monitor

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

#define GPIO_PIN        17
#define LOG_FILE        "motor_rpm.log"
#define DEBOUNCE_US     2000   /* 2 ms */
#define POLL_INTERVAL_S 5
#define MAX_PULSES      100

static volatile sig_atomic_t g_running = 1;

static void sig_handler(int sig)
{
    (void)sig;
    g_running = 0;
}

/*
 * Read the current monotonic clock value in microseconds.
 * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error.
 */
static long long read_clock_us(void)
{
    struct timespec ts;
    if (clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &ts) != 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    return (long long)ts.tv_sec * 1000000LL + ts.tv_nsec / 1000LL;
}

/*
 * Count pulses on the GPIO line and return the total count.
 * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error.
 */
static int count_pulses(void)
{
    int count = 0;
    int last_state = 0;
    int prev_state = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < MAX_PULSES && g_running; i++) {
        int state = gpio_get_value(GPIO_PIN);
        if (state < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "gpio_get_value failed on GPIO %d: %s\n",
                    GPIO_PIN, strerror(errno));
            return -1;
        }
        if (state != prev_state) {
            count++;
            prev_state = state;
        }
        usleep(DEBOUNCE_US);
    }
    return count;
}

/*
 * Compute the motor RPM from the pulse count.
 * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error.
 */
static int compute_rpm(int pulse_count)
{
    if (pulse_count < 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    long long elapsed_us = read_clock_us() - DEBOUNCE_US;
    if (elapsed_us <= 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    return (int)((double)pulse_count * 60.0 / elapsed_us);
}

/*
 * Append a timestamped RPM value to the log file.
 * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error.
 */
static int log_rpm(int rpm)
{
    FILE *fp = fopen(LOG_FILE, "a");
    if (!fp) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error opening log file '%s': %s\n",
                LOG_FILE, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }

    time_t t = time(NULL);
    if (t == (time_t)-1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "time() failed: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        fclose(fp);
        return -1;
    }

    struct tm tm_info;
    if (localtime_r(&t, &tm_info) == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "localtime_r() failed\n");
        fclose(fp);
        return -1;
    }

    char timestamp[32];
    if (strftime(timestamp, sizeof(timestamp), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S", &tm_info) == 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "strftime() failed\n");
        fclose(fp);
        return -1;
    }

    if (fprintf(fp, "%s,%.2f\n", timestamp, rpm) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "fprintf to log failed: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        fclose(fp);
        return -1;
    }

    if (fclose(fp) != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "fclose() failed: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }

    return 0;
}

/*
 * RPM monitor for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using an A3144 Hall-effect sensor
 * and a two-pole magnet on the motor shaft.
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   A3144 VCC  -> 3.3 V (pin 1)
 *   A3144 GND  -> GND  (pin 6)
 *   A3144 OUT  -> GPIO17 (BCM 17, physical pin 11)
 *   Magnet N/S  -> GPIO17 (BCM 17)
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o rpm_monitor rpm_monitor.c -lrt
 * Run:    ./rpm_monitor
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <sys/ioctl.h>
#include <linux/gpio.h>

#define GPIO_PIN        17
#define LOG_FILE        "motor_rpm.log"
#define DEBOUNCE_US     2000   /* 2 ms */
#define POLL_INTERVAL_S 5
#define MAX_PULSES      100

static volatile sig_atomic_t g_running = 1;

static void sig_handler(int sig)
{
    (void)sig;
    g_running = 0;
}

/*
 * Read the current monotonic clock value in microseconds.
 * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error.
 */
static long long read_clock_us(void)
{
    struct timespec ts;
    if (clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &ts) != 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    return (long long)ts.tv_sec * 1000000LL + ts.tv_nsec / 1000LL;
}

/*
 * Count pulses on the GPIO line and return the total count.
 * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error.
 */
static int count_pulses(void)
{
    int count = 0;
    int last_state = 0;
    int prev_state = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < MAX_PULSES && g_running; i++) {
        int state = gpio_get_value(GPIO_PIN);
        if (state < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "gpio_get_value failed on GPIO %d: %s\n",
                    GPIO_PIN, strerror(errno));
            return -1;
        }
        if (state != prev_state) {
            count++;
            prev_state = state;
        }
        usleep(DEBOUNCE_US);
    }
    return count;
}

/*
 * Compute the motor RPM from the pulse count.
 * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error.
 */
static int compute_rpm(int pulse_count)
{
    if (pulse_count < 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    long long elapsed_us = read_clock_us() - DEBOUNCE_US;
    if (elapsed_us <= 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    return (int)((double)pulse_count * 60.0 / elapsed_us);
}

/*
 * Append a timestamped RPM value to the log file.
 * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error.
 */
static int log_rpm(int rpm)
{
    FILE *fp = fopen(LOG_FILE, "a");
    if (!fp) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error opening log file '%s': %s\n",
                LOG_FILE, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }

    time_t t = time(NULL);
    if (t == (time_t)-1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "time() failed: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        fclose(fp);
        return -1;
    }

    struct tm tm_info;
    if (localtime_r(&t, &tm_info) == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "localtime_r() failed\n");
        fclose(fp);
        return -1;
    }

    char timestamp[32];
    if (strftime(timestamp, sizeof(timestamp), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S", &tm_info) == 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "strftime() failed\n");
        fclose(fp);
        return -1;
    }

    if (fprintf(fp, "%s,%.2f\n", timestamp, rpm) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "fprintf to log failed: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        fclose(fp);
        return -1;
    }

    if (fclose(fp) != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "fclose() failed: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }

    return 0;
}

int main(void)
{
    /* Install signal handlers for clean shutdown */
    struct sigaction sa;
    memset(&sa, 0, sizeof(sa));
    sa.sa_handler = sig_handler;
    sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
    sa.sa_flags = 0;

    if (sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL) != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "sigaction(SIGINT) failed: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    if (sigaction(SIGTERM, &sa, NULL) != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "sigaction(SIGTERM) failed: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /* Open the log file in append mode */
    int log_fd = open(LOG_FILE, O_WRONLY | O_APPEND | O_CREAT, 0644);
    if (log_fd < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error opening log file '%s': %s\n",
                LOG_FILE, strerror(errno));
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /* Configure GPIO pin as input with internal pull-up */

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements a timed water distribution schedule for two Adafruit Solenoid Valves, Product ID 997, each driven through a relay module on the GPIO bus, with Valve 1’s relay connected to GPIO 17 (BCM) and Valve 2’s relay connected to GPIO 18 (BCM); the program must repeatedly activate Valve 1 for 500 ms then pause 5 seconds, activate Valve 2 for 1000 ms then pause 10 seconds, logging every activation event with an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named valve_log.txt, include robust error handling for GPIO chip initialization failures, line request failures, and file I/O errors, and install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that ensure clean release of all GPIO lines and closure of the log file on exit, while observing that each 12 V, 0.7 A valve is controlled only via its relay (GPIO HIGH = relay ON = valve OPEN, GPIO LOW = relay OFF = valve CLOSED) and the schedule repeats indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the I2C bus 1 (SDA = GPIO2, SCL = GPIO3) to communicate with an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor, initializing the MPR121 in stop mode, configuring touch and release thresholds for all twelve electrodes, setting the filter and charge time as well as the electrode current, then switching the device into run mode after a 100 ms stabilization delay; the program must monitor the touch status and, whenever any electrode reports a touch (touch_status > 0), toggle a relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM) and print the relay toggle status to the output, loop with a 100 ms delay between iterations, implement robust error handling for every I2C transaction, GPIO operation and any initialization failure, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C interface and terminates the driver usage.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that monitors an HC‑SR501 PIR sensor on GPIO 17 (BCM numbering, configured as an input with a pull‑down) and controls an electric door strike relay on GPIO 18 (BCM, configured as an output) via the GPIO bus, using a single‑threaded, non‑blocking polling loop with a 50 ms interval to detect a rising edge from 0 to 1; on each motion detection the program must activate the relay for exactly 500 ms to momentarily unlock the door strike, then enforce rate limiting by ignoring any further motion events for 2 seconds after each unlock, while writing millisecond‑precision timestamps to a file named door_events.log for every motion detected, door unlocked, and rate‑limited event; if the driver library fails to initialize the program must print a clear error message and exit with status 1; on normal termination or receipt of SIGINT the program must clean up by closing the log file, terminating the driver library, and ensuring the relay is set to off.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that generates randomized haptic feedback patterns on two Precision Microdrives 310-101 eccentric rotating mass (ERM) vibration motors connected via GPIO (PWM), with Motor 1 driven on GPIO 17 (BCM) and Motor 2 on GPIO 27 (BCM); each pattern must consist of a sequence of 5 to 15 steps, each step specifying a PWM duty cycle from 0 to 255 for each motor and a step duration between 50 ms and 200 ms, using the appropriate API calls for PWM control and timing, seeding the random number generator with time(NULL), checking the API call return values, verifying that the GPIO mode is set correctly, handling any memory allocation failures, and running indefinitely to generate and play new random patterns until a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) is received, at which point a volatile sig_atomic_t shutdown flag should trigger a graceful shutdown that stops both motors and releases all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a weight‑triggered solenoid lock using a load cell amplified by an HX711 on the GPIO bus, with the HX711 data line connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the clock line to GPIO17 (BCM), and the solenoid lock driven by GPIO27 (BCM) as an active‑high lock signal; the program must read the HX711 sensor every 500 ms, enforce a read timeout of 0.5 seconds and gracefully skip any iteration where the timeout occurs, initialize the GPIO driver with error checking, load calibration data (scale_factor and offset) from a space‑separated calibration.txt file or fall back to defaults of scale = 1.0 and offset = 0.0 if the file is missing or invalid, perform a one‑time startup calibration by averaging 100 readings at zero load to determine the offset, compute weight using the loaded or default scale and offset, engage the solenoid (set GPIO27 high) when the computed weight exceeds a calibrated threshold of 10.0 kg, log each reading with a timestamp to weight_log.txt and write any updated calibration values back to calibration.txt, and handle SIGINT to cleanly shut down by releasing all GPIO resources and closing open files.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a Seeed Studio Grove Rain Sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM) on the GPIO bus, debouncing by taking five readings spaced 50 ms apart and declaring rain when at least three of those readings are LOW (the sensor outputs LOW when rain is present and HIGH when dry); when rain is detected the program must drive a DC motor through an L298N motor driver using IN1 on GPIO17 (BCM), IN2 on GPIO18 (BCM) and the PWM enable line on GPIO27 (BCM), setting IN1 high, IN2 low and applying a 1000 Hz PWM signal with a duty cycle value of 150 (out of 0‑255) for exactly five seconds to close the window, then stopping the motor by clearing IN1, IN2 and PWM, logging each rain event and each motor action with timestamps to /var/log/window_control.log via syslog, checking the sensor only once every 60 seconds and waiting an additional 60 seconds after a closing operation before the next check, handling any GPIO initialization failures with clear error messages and distinct exit codes, providing robust error handling for all sensor reads and motor control actions, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM the motor is stopped, all GPIO resources are released, and the log file is properly closed for a graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a kitchen ingredient stock level using a TAL220B load cell amplified by an HX711 connected on the GPIO bus with bit‑banged communication, reading the data line (DT) on GPIO23 (BCM) and the clock line (SCK) on GPIO24 (BCM), checking the weight once every second, and when the measured weight falls below 100 g it must activate a solenoid lock attached to GPIO17 (BCM) for exactly five seconds; each weight check, lock activation, and any error condition—including HX711 read timeouts, a data line stuck high, GPIO operation failures, or file I/O problems—must be logged with a timestamp to a file named stock_events.txt, and the program must implement robust error handling for all reads, writes, and file operations and perform proper resource cleanup when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads weight from an HX711 load cell amplifier using a bit‑banged GPIO bus with the data line on GPIO4 (BCM) and the clock line on GPIO17 (BCM), applying clock high/low delays of at least 1 µs, and obtains raw 24‑bit signed values; at startup the program must prompt the user to place a known weight, compute and save a calibration factor to a file named calibration.txt, then continuously sample the sensor, treating a data line that remains high for more than 100 ms as a communication timeout, and when the calibrated weight exceeds a threshold of 5.0 kg the program must engage a solenoid door lock connected to GPIO27 (BCM) by setting the pin high for exactly 5 seconds before releasing it, log the timestamp and weight to a file called security.log each time the threshold is exceeded, and robustly handle driver initialization failures, file open or write errors, calibration read errors, and HX711 timeouts; a SIGINT handler must be provided to gracefully unlock the solenoid, terminate the driver, close any open files and release all resources on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors a Keywish KY‑022 IR obstacle avoidance sensor connected to GPIO16 (BCM) on the GPIO bus and toggles a Songle SRD‑05VDC‑SL relay module attached to GPIO20 (BCM) accordingly, logging each state change with the new relay state (ON or OFF) and an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named relay_events.log; the sensor is active‑low so a LOW reading indicates an obstacle and must cause the relay, which is active‑high, to switch from its current state to the opposite state, and the implementation must use only the provided driver library APIs for all GPIO operations, must detect and report initialization failures such as chip not found or line request failed, must detect and report sensor read errors and log file write errors with descriptive messages, must clean up all GPIO resources on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM before exiting, and must ensure that every toggle event is recorded in the log file as specified.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors an HC‑SR501 PIR sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM) on the GPIO bus, and when the sensor’s active‑high 3.3 V output indicates motion, activates a 5 V buzzer on GPIO18 (BCM) for exactly 2 seconds using usleep for timing, then returns the buzzer to the off state; each motion detection must be logged by appending a line with the timestamp in the format YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS to a file named motion_log.txt, and every call to the GPIO driver API must be checked for errors so that a missing sensor or bus error causes a clear error message and clean program exit; the program must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turn off the buzzer, close the log file, and release all GPIO resources before terminating, and it should run indefinitely until the user presses Ctrl‑C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a timed watering system by activating a Parker Hannifin Series 9 General Purpose Miniature Solenoid Valve (12 V, 1.6 W) through an external N‑channel MOSFET or relay module connected to GPIO18 (BCM) on the GPIO bus; the program must read the watering duration, constrained to 1–3600 seconds, from a configuration file named watering.conf that contains a single line of the form duration=<seconds>, reject empty files, malformed lines, or out‑of‑range values, initialize the GPIO line as an output with active‑low = 0 and a default low value (valve off), activate the valve by setting the line high, wait the configured duration using a signal‑safe interruptible sleep, then set the line low, print status messages to stdout showing the configured duration and each valve on/off transition, perform error handling by checking every driver call for errors and printing descriptive messages to stderr, install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, have the main loop poll this flag and turn the valve off before exiting, and ensure that on every exit path—whether normal completion, signal receipt, or error—the GPIO line is released and the chip closed so the valve is always left off.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that controls a line‑following robot using a Keywish 3‑Way Infrared Tracking Sensor and two DC motors driven through an L298N motor driver, communicating over the GPIO / PWM bus; the left sensor must be read from GPIO4 (BCM), the middle sensor from GPIO17 (BCM), the right sensor from GPIO27 (BCM), and the motor PWM signals must be output on GPIO22, GPIO23, GPIO24 and GPIO25 (BCM), with all three sensor inputs sampled every 10 ms and the PWM signals generated at a 1 kHz frequency, while the sensors provide active‑low digital signals and the control law requires that when the middle sensor is low the robot drives straight at a base speed of 150 out of 255, when only the left sensor is low the robot turns right by halving the left motor speed, when only the right sensor is low it turns left by halving the right motor speed, and when no sensor is low both motors are stopped; each control cycle must be logged to a file named trace_log.txt with an ISO 8601 timestamp, the three sensor states (0/1), and the left and right motor speeds, and the implementation must include robust error handling for initializing the driver library, opening the log file, and all GPIO operations, and must install a SIGINT handler that on receipt stops both motors, closes the log file, terminates the driver library and ensures that all driver library API calls are properly released before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads illuminance from a BH1750 light sensor on I2C bus 1, observes a 180 ms measurement delay, and drives a relay connected to GPIO23 (BCM) to turn on a grow lamp whenever the lux reading falls below 150, logging each lux value and every relay state change with millisecond‑precision timestamps to a file named grow_log.txt; the program must handle I2C errors gracefully by logging any sensor detection or read failures and continuing operation without crashing, run indefinitely until a SIGINT is received, and on that signal cleanly release all resources by closing the I2C handle, turning off the relay, and terminating the driver library, using only C and standard POSIX APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a door lock using the library's API call to drive a servo motor on the GPIO/PWM bus, with the servo connected to GPIO18 (BCM) and two push‑buttons connected to GPIO21 (BCM) for lock and GPIO22 (BCM) for unlock, both using pull‑up resistors and active‑low logic (reading 0 when pressed); the program must debounce each button press with a 100 ms delay, set the servo pulse width to 1000 µs (≈0°) when the lock button is pressed and to 2000 µs (≈180°) when the unlock button is pressed while respecting the API’s safe pulse‑width range of 500‑2500 µs, print status messages for each action, handle any initialization failures gracefully by printing an error message, and install a SIGINT signal handler that cleanly releases all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that generates a haptic feedback system by pulsing two Precision Microdrives 310‑101 vibration motors sequentially and repeatedly over the GPIO bus, driving motor 1 through a driver circuit attached to GPIO17 (BCM) for 200 ms, then motor 2 through a driver circuit attached to GPIO27 (BCM) for 300 ms, and looping this pattern indefinitely; the design must include robust error handling that checks every driver library call for line request failures and value write failures, as well as proper registration of signal handlers, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully release the GPIO lines and stop the motors by invoking the library’s API call() on all exit paths, while observing the constraint that the motors require 3 V at 60 mA typical and therefore must be driven through an external driver circuit such as an NPN transistor with a flyback diode rather than being connected directly to the GPIO pins.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that implements a sound‑triggered alarm as a single executable with two selectable modes chosen by a command‑line argument; in the sound_sensor mode the program polls the LM393 sound sensor on its digital output pin connected to GPIO17 (BCM) every 10 ms, treats a logic 0 on this active‑low pin as a sound event, and publishes an alert on a ZeroMQ socket bound to tcp://*:5555 using the topic SOUND_ALERTS, while in the alarm_node mode the program subscribes to tcp://localhost:5555 for the same topic and, upon receiving a message, lights an alarm LED attached to GPIO27 (BCM) for exactly 1 second; the implementation must use the GPIO bus directly without any driver library, provide robust error handling for every GPIO and ZeroMQ call, and install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that perform a clean shutdown by releasing the GPIO lines, the GPIO chip, and all ZeroMQ sockets and context on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses an IR receiver such as the TSOP38238 connected to GPIO17 (BCM) to decode NEC infrared remote signals and report the decoded commands both to syslog and to an MQTT broker at localhost on port 1883 using the topic ir/decoded, publishing the command as a JSON object; the program must register an alert callback on the falling edge of the GPIO to capture pulse timings, interpret the NEC frame consisting of a 9 ms mark followed by a 4.5 ms space header, 560 µs marks for each bit, a 1690 µs space for logic‑1 and a 560 µs space for logic‑0, decode the full 32‑bit frame, validate the command against its inverted copy while allowing extended NEC frames that omit inverted‑address validation, check driver initialization and GPIO setup failures, guard against pulse‑buffer overflow, verify the NEC checksum, initialize the MQTT client once at startup and invoke the network loop in the main loop, and ensure clean release of all resources—including the driver, MQTT client, and syslog—when the process receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads ambient light from four BH1750FVI sensors attached to I2C‑1, waiting 180 ms after each start‑conversion command, and repeats this acquisition loop once per second; for each sensor the program must issue an ioctl(I2C_SLAVE, addr) before any transaction, may use a single /dev/i2c-1 descriptor or one per sensor, and must not rely on any external driver library, handling any open, address‑set, write, read or partial‑read failure by inserting a NaN value for that sensor while continuing with the others; after gathering the lux values it must broadcast a UDP multicast packet to 239.255.255.250:5005 containing a semicolon‑separated list of sensor_id,lux pairs such as 1,120.5;2,85.0;3,210.5;4,45.0, and it must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a termination flag so the loop can exit cleanly, ensuring that all file descriptors for I2C and the UDP socket are closed on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that opens the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1, issues a zero‑length I2C write to generate a start condition and then reads two bytes from the Honeywell AWM7300V mass airflow sensor, masks the 14‑bit flow value from the first two bytes according to the sensor documentation, converts it to SLPM, and logs a timestamped flow‑rate entry to a file named airflow_log.txt once per second; the program must check the result of every system call, retry any transient I2C read failure up to three times with a 100 ms delay between attempts, and handle the distinct error paths for a missing sensor (ENXIO) and a bus error (EIO), and it must install a SIGINT handler that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and flushes and closes the log file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads spectral and lux data from an Adafruit AS7341 10‑Channel Light/Color Sensor attached to the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) for plant health monitoring, verifying that the sensor’s identification register matches the documented value, powering the device on by setting the PON bit in the ENABLE register, configuring the SMUX through the CFG6 register, and enabling spectral measurement with the SP_EN bit, then acquiring all ten spectral channels (F1‑F8, Clear and NIR) every five seconds, computing a simplified lux approximation from those readings, and appending a timestamped, comma‑separated line to spectral_log.csv at the same interval while checking every I2C read/write return value and handling cases where the sensor is absent or the bus fails, and finally ensuring that all resources—including the I2C file descriptor and the log file—are cleanly closed on normal termination or when a SIGINT is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads tri‑axial acceleration data from an Omron D7S seismic sensor over the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) and logs the timestamped X, Y, Z values in g to a CSV file named seismic_data.csv by default, with columns timestamp,x_g,y_g,z_g, while also writing any error messages with timestamps to seismic_error.log; the program must accept a command‑line option ‑a to specify the I2C address (defaulting to the documented value), ‑i to set the sampling interval in seconds (default 1 s), and ‑f to set the output filename (default seismic_data.csv), perform reads at the configured interval, check every I2C read/write return value, retry transient failures up to three times with a 10 ms backoff, detect sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by closing the I2C file descriptor and flushing and closing the CSV file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the ambient light from a BH1750 light sensor attached to the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) once every second, converts the 16‑bit big‑endian raw value to a floating‑point lux value, and broadcasts that value as a floating‑point string via UDP multicast to 239.255.255.250:5000 with a TTL of 1; the program must check every I2C write and read operation for failure, and if the sensor is absent or a bus error occurs it should print an error message and retry after one second, and it must install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the socket before exiting, using only the Linux I2C ioctl interface and standard POSIX sockets, and run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with a Texas Instruments AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor over UART (/dev/ttyS0) at 921600 baud, reads the sensor’s data stream, synchronizes on the documented 8‑byte little‑endian magic word, validates each TLV payload, extracts the range (in meters) and velocity (in meters per second) for every detected object, and appends rows to a file named radar_data.csv with the columns timestamp, object_index, range_m, velocity_mps; the program must check every UART read, handle partial reads and buffer overflows gracefully, skip malformed frames, log any errors to stderr without crashing, and on all exit paths including SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly release resources by closing the UART using the provided driver library, flushing and closing the CSV file, and invoking the library’s call() cleanup function.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64‑bit OS that periodically reads range‑detection data from a Texas Instruments AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor over UART (/dev/serial0, GPIO14/GPIO15 BCM pins as TXD/RXD) at 115200 baud, 8N1, using a 0.5 second inter‑byte timeout and a select() call with a 2‑second timeout to detect sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions; the program must open and configure the UART in non‑canonical mode, accumulate partial reads into a line buffer, parse only complete newline‑terminated ASCII lines of the form `<unix_timestamp_seconds>,<range_meters>\n`, and for each valid detection log to stdout exactly as “Timestamp: YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Range: X.XX meters”, while checking the result of every system call (open, tcgetattr, tcsetattr, read, select, strdup) and printing errno‑based diagnostics on failure, and must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to ensure a graceful shutdown that closes the UART on all exit paths, using only standard POSIX C libraries such as stdio, stdlib, string, fcntl, unistd, errno, sys/select, signal, and time.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the Keywish 3‑Way Tracking Sensor (KY‑033) connected on the GPIO bus, configuring the left sensor pin as GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7), the middle sensor pin as GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) and the right sensor pin as GPIO27 (BCM, physical pin 13) as inputs with pull‑up resistors enabled, noting that each sensor output is digital LOW when an obstacle is present and HIGH when clear, and runs a main loop at 10 Hz (100 ms period) that logs the three sensor states to the console with a timestamp using 0 for obstacle detected and 1 for clear, and when all three sensors read 0 the program must send the string “EMERGENCY STOP!\n” over the library’s API call to the UART device /dev/ttyAMA0 configured at 115200 baud, 8N1 with no flow control; the program must check the driver library initialization and, on failure, print an error and exit with code 1, while any failure of the API call should be reported with an error message but the program must continue running, handling write errors gracefully by printing the error without exiting; signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM must close the UART port, terminate the driver library and release all resources before exiting, and any error path must also clean up all allocated resources.
